items.title: 'The last jersey I still wanted and needed' – Champion of championships Remco Evenepoel completes the set with eighth elite title out of eight
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Remco Evenepoel is undeniably one of the greatest riders of this ongoing generation, but as he added the UEC European Championships road race title to his already illustrious palmarès in Slovenia, the Belgian completed the set of winning all eight championship titles available to him.

Across the two disciplines of the road race and individual time trial, at just 26, Evenepoel has now won both at the Belgian National Championships, European Championships, World Championships, and the Olympic Games, in a run spanning back seven years, with 24 medals won at the elite level.

In an era mostly dominated by one rider, Tadej Pogačar, Evenepoel's talents as a time trial expert and elite one-day racer, long known since he burst onto the scene as a junior, have seen him go on to achieve a level of completion the Slovenian has only managed half of.

And looking back to 2018, just 18 months after he had become a cyclist, is it any real surprise? At the Europeans Championships, he did the double in the junior road race and time trial in Zlín, Czechia, before netting an unprecedented double double as he achieved the same feat at the World Championships in Innsbruck, winning both junior rainbow jerseys by more than 1:20.

Even as an inexperienced teenager, Evenepoel was the master of championships, and this latest feat and completion of the championship bingo only adds to his legacy as a rider for the big occasion.

"This jersey is added to my list of achievements, but you played a big part in that. A huge thank you for that," he added that evening, in his speech to the Belgian team and staff. "The same goes for the staff. Everything was well organised again. Thanks to everyone who contributed even a little bit.

"And I think I'm not riding championships anymore now, right?" he joked. "No, that's not true."

His first major elite title came at the Europeans a year after his junior dominance, vindicating his early step up to the professional level as he beat specialists Kasper Asgreen, Edoardo Affini, Stefan Küng, Alex Dowsett and Filippo Ganna to the title in Alkmaar at just 19.

Evenepoel's next gold medal came at the Belgian Championships, but not until 2022, with his major crash at Il Lombardia in 2020 stunting some of his inevitable progress. He beat then-teammate Yves Lampaert convincingly to the time trial title in Gavere.

Fast forward three months and Evenepoel became road race World Champion in Wollongong, claiming the rainbow jersey by more than two minutes after he went solo in the last 25km.

In 2023, he added two more major titles, winning the Belgian national road race title ahead of Alec Segaert in Izegem, before going on to win the first of his four World titles in the elite time trial, scorching to victory in Stirling after finishing on the podium in his first three attempts.

He made history a season later, becoming the first male rider to do the double at the Olympic Games in Paris, dominating the race against the clock, before claiming an iconic solo win in the road race. With the help of Wout van Aert marking Mathieu van der Poel up the Montmartre climb, Evenepoel was able to time his attack to perfection, surviving despite a late bike change, and celebrating in front of the Eiffel Tower.

With this feat achieved, Evenepoel's tally of championship wins was already at seven, with just the European road race remaining on his hit list. Before the race in Ljubljana, Evenepoel had gone close twice to completing the eight, losing out to Sonny Colbrelli in a two-up sprint in Trento in 2021, and only being beaten by Pogačar in France a season ago.

Lining up at the start with Pogačar still out injured, Evenepoel was the heavy favourite to claim the iconic European jersey, but as is typical of the Belgians' entire career, it was never going to be as simple as him riding off solo into the sunset.

The Italian team mounted a major challenge, upping the pace for their big leaders Giulio Ciccone and Christian Scaroni, and just as the race started to really heat up and Evenepoel began his move on the Možjanca climb, with Ciccone following him, the Belgian crashed.

A week after the disappointment of failing to deliver at the World Championships, Evenepoel's hope of the eighth was looking like it might go up in smoke, but with luck on his side, his bike wasn't badly broken, and his teammates were just coming up to help dig him out of the hole.

Maxim van Gils and Ramses Debruyne brought him back to the front, and the next time up, he was able to put the hammer down again. But still, the race wasn't done, with Ciccone able to follow and then staying – for the vast majority of the run for home – in the stronger rider's wheel.

Not only did it take a two-up sprint to decide the day, but one of the closest photo finishes in recent memory confirmed Evenepoel was the champion, narrowly pipping Ciccone with an expert bike throw by the barest of margins in Šenčur. Not only did he complete the set, but Evenepoel had righted the wrongs of Montreal.

"I might not have really shown it, but I was still very disappointed in myself and my performance. I also felt like I had disappointed the whole country with my performance," he said. "I still hope that everyone is proud now that we are back. And sorry again for last week's World Championship. Now I'm going to celebrate this one big time."

Evenepoel travelled back to Belgium today, but will be on the road once again on Wednesday, "Because there is another important race on Saturday," as he heads for Italy to take on Il Lombardia. Second in the past two seasons behind Pogačar, Evenepoel will be the favourite for the Monument and will look to close out a successful 2026 season with a bang.

items.title: Visma-Lease a Bike promote former rider Nathan Van Hooydonck to new leading sporting director role
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike have announced that Nathan Van Hooydonck has been promoted to a new role as sporting director.

Van Hooydonck, whose last race came at the 2023 Tour of Britain, initially transitioned to work as a VIP guest guide during major races throughout the season. In October 2024, he took up the commercial role, and now, he steps up to a position as leader of Visma's Sport Management Team (SMT).

"Nathan is still young, but incredibly eager to learn and someone who feels completely connected to this team and to what we want to achieve together," said Visma-Lease a Bike CEO Richard Plugge.

"He not only knows our culture, he acts according to it and embodies it. For years, I have also seen how determined he is to win and how much it means to him when we do not. As a former rider, he also has the credibility to have an opinion on the sport and to express it.

"Through his experience within the Business Team, he has quickly learned to look beyond the sporting side of things and to see the connection with the rest of our organisation.

"That gives us confidence that he will do a very good job in this role. And he certainly will not be doing it alone. With people such as Mathieu Heijboer, who has been and will continue to be an important part of our organisation, Nathan can draw on a great deal of knowledge and experience."

Visma say that Van Hooydonck will take responsibility for "defining and overseeing the team's key sporting objectives." Van Hooydonck, who turns 31 next week, will also "safeguard the long-term vision, values and culture" of the team.

Van Hooydonck joins Plugge, Marc Reef, Mathieu Heijboer, Robbert de Groot, and Patrick Broe on Visma's SMT. As part of the setup, he'll be partly responsible for ensuring the squad can continue to challenge and beat bigger budget squads, including UAE Team Emirates-XRG.

He said that his time spent on the commercial side of Visma allowed him to see the team "from a different perspective."

"It has helped me to better understand the organisation and experience how all the different parts are connected. Richard has also played a huge role in my development and in giving me the opportunity I now have to take on this role within the team," said Van Hooydonck.

"Ultimately, for me, it comes down to one thing: winning. To achieve that, we need to move in the same direction as an organisation every single day. That means being willing to challenge each other, to push each other and, at the same time, to make sure everyone feels involved in what we are trying to achieve together. I am really looking forward to contributing to that from this role."

Van Hooydonck isn't the first change at Visma for the 2027 season. So far, the men's team has brought on board neo-pro Matisse Van Kerckhove and Mark Donovan (Pinarello-Q36.5), while the women's squad will welcome Femke Markus (SD Worx-Protime) and Maike van der Duijn (Canyon-SRAM).

On the staff side, head of the sport management team Jacco Verhaeren is on the outgoing list, with the team having announced his departure "decided in consultation with the team" back in September. After the surprise departure of head of racing Grischa Niermann, announced back in June, Reef stepped up into that role on September 1 and will carry that into 2027.

items.title: Japanese Grand Prix 2026 MotoGP rider rankings
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
The two main MotoGP title contenders separated themselves from the field again in the Japanese Grand Prix at Motegi - but does Marc Marquez's 37-pointer warrant P1 in the rankings, or is there another candidate?

2nd 1st 1st

One of the easier P1 selections this year (and Marquez's fourth this season, for reference).

The Ducati didn't have the clear edge over the Aprilia at Motegi some may have expected - but Marquez did have a clear edge over everyone else.

Friday to Saturday to Sunday, he was simply too strong - too in tune with the various twists of the weekend with the new surface and revised allocation, too comfortable running at consistent top pace, too precise in turning P2 into P1 in both races.

1st 3rd 2nd

Championship-spec Jorge Martin is turning up here, though Marquez has shown that won't necessarily be enough.

But Friday had promised a much more damaging weekend for Martin - who needed Pedro Acosta's help to ensure a Q2 spot - and yet he turned it around completely with an "unbelievable" overnight improvement.

Excessive tyre spin cost him on Saturday - he was maybe unlucky (and maybe careless) to touch the green paint on the final lap, but was anyway lucky that other strong riders had been taken out.

Sunday, then, was really, really good - even though keeping Marquez behind for the full distance always seemed impossible.

7th 4th 4th

A throwback to both mid-2025 Enea Bastianini (the one who could briefly make the KTM work) and to Ducati-era Bastianini (who would occasionally deliver mind-bending laps at the end of the race).

The biggest breakthrough, I think, was actually in navigating Friday and then qualifying well - though probably this was just a reflection of a higher-overall level of performance by Bastianini this weekend.

When he's fast over one lap, you know he'll be fast over a race distance. And he was, with only the finest margins separating him from podium finishes.

Acosta's DNF in the sprint complicates intra-KTM comparisons somewhat, but the 14.6s gap between them at the finish on Sunday leaves little doubt Bastianini was the RC16 benchmark this time.

12th9th 12th

Fabio Quartararo has been one of MotoGP's best riders again since the embarrassment of Aragon at the end of August.

What appears to be a minor underperformance in qualifying - relative to his own standards, because he obliterated the other Yamahas again - means it wasn't a hugely eye-catching weekend, but it was a really professional one.

He rode a strong sprint in fending off Fermin Aldeguer for the final point, and was the Yamaha standard-bearer in the main race, too - though was limited by excessive fuel consumption from very early on, a common Yamaha issue but one that seems to affect him more than some of his peers.

15th 14th 13th

This was a delightful MotoGP redemption weekend for Somkiat Chantra, whose 2025 in the category quickly devolved into a waste of everyone's time - but who, though his exit was totally justified, is better than that year suggested.

He found a bike on which "everything was correct" from the first run, tweaking only some engine brake settings for a couple of corners, and was properly competitive, just three tenths off the best Honda in qualifying and beating team-mate Luca Marini.

He looked more than a little timid in the early phase of both races - and apparently got roughed up a little by Johann Zarco on Sunday, before recovering well into the points.

The only caveat is that I felt similarly good about Taka Nakagami's stand-in effort at the previous race - and I think it's fair to ask whether Honda's regulars need to do some soul-searching about the performance they're bringing to the table.

4th 6th 3rd

The roll of the dice on medium tyres for the sprint was the biggest issue with Marco Bezzecchi's weekend - as, despite not encountering the same awful blistering as fellow medium-tyre runner Jack Miller, he simply had no pace and came home in a sixth position flattered by attrition.

Good pace on the same tyre earlier in the day meant there was some logic, but the gamble backfired.

Yet equally surprising was that, having seemingly arrived into the weekend on top of Martin and the other Aprilias, Bezzecchi suddenly had no answer to his team-mate in the most important sessions.

But also, these 20 points could have been zero. He very nearly had the same crash in the damp early in FP1 that took Nakagami out of the weekend.

8th 8th 5th

Raul Fernandez came to Motegi with lingering worry about his performance at so-called 'stop-and-go' tracks this season - and was relentlessly positive about his feeling on the weekend in that context.

He was struggling on corner entry on Friday but had underlying top-10 performance comfortably and showed it on the other two days, with the grand prix ride to fifth under pressure from Acosta and Ai Ogura particularly impressive (also because he had to manage "very big consumption" on the fuel side).

9th 2nd DNF

The Sunday crash, from "just touching the throttle and losing the front" while not really pushing, took the shine off the weekend - but the Saturday podium was more valuable to Diogo Moreira and Honda than any realistic result on Sunday would have been.

"One of the most talented riders I've ever seen, riding every different type of bike," good friend Marc Marquez raved, referencing Moreira's abundance of dirt-track skill but also, of course, his performance in MotoGP so far this season.

Add to it that he was fresh off surgery to remove a screw from his left wrist, and that puts some extra gloss on the achievement.

3rd DNF 7th

At a track where so much was expected of Acosta, he places the lowest he's been in these rankings since Jerez five months ago. That reflects, more than anything, the fact that for the first time in a really long time someone within KTM had his number - which will be easier to take after the Austria win.

Acosta cannily latched on to Bezzecchi in Q2 to secure a front row start, but didn't capitalise in either race.

He says the principal issue on Sunday was simply a mismatch between his bike and the hard rear tyre - but admitted that alone can't explain "that Enea was that fast and I was that slow".

Obviously the sprint was a write-off due to the Alex Marquez induced pile-up - but he was in the firing line to begin with because he was being overtaken by Bastianini.

11th 5th 6th

Fourth of four Aprilias in most sessions, Ogura looked more like you would have expected he would at his first race back post-injury in Austria a fortnight ago - though still he was never terribly far off.

He battled locking on Friday and lacked acceleration on Sunday, which didn't help to get through on Trackhouse team-mate Fernandez (the "messy" battle with Acosta didn't, either).

But it was a healthy return of points in the end (thanks also to a strong sprint), given he seemingly just wasn't really in the groove.

6th DNF 18th

Somewhat of a 'default' ranking for Fabio Di Giannantonio, who was banged up through zero fault of his own after the multi-bike crash in the sprint.

He was putting together a fairly promising weekend before that (though left it until the last second to secure a Friday top-10), but just wasn't fit to achieve anything much after the "big hit" to his ribs and hip on the right side.

13th DNF 8th

It was a far, far, far-far-far cry from the heights of his 2025 outlier glory weekend, but did look more like the respectable Austria than the truly dreadful Pecco Bagnaia weekends that came right before.

He made a Q1 error but the pure pace was Q2-marginal at best, and the sprint wasn't going anywhere great before he so dramatically ran out of rear rubber.

In all that context, the grand prix was quite good - but the contrast to last year was upsetting for Bagnaia. "It's not a lack of feeling," he insisted. "I cannot do what the fastest riders do."

18th 10th 9th

Aldeguer, who had had leg surgery in the lead-up to Motegi in the hopes of aiding his continued recovery from the off-season femur fracture, probably should have run with Acosta and the Trackhouse riders - but made his own weekend too difficult.

He narrowly missed out on a Q2 spot on Friday - 0.004s the difference - and then botched Q1, lapping slower than the day before and placing himself on row six.

Options were limited from there, as Aldeguer made tidy but unremarkable progress.

16th 11th 10th

Marini had to salvage a "really bad" weekend, which was compromised by a seemingly innocuous early crash on Friday afternoon - that cost him a key tyre set, he lost feeling and even when the opportunity presented itself to follow Marc Marquez for a fast lap, he couldn't capitalise.

He was outmatched in Q1 again and quiet in the sprint but found joy in the hard rear on Sunday, smoothing things over with a 10th place as, somehow, Honda's top finisher - which he so often is without having lights-out pace.

21st 13th 16th

Alex Rins's weekend was unfortunately more notable for the showy lift he got from Miller than anything he could do on track.

Crashing on his first flying lap on Friday afternoon probably didn't help, but ultimately it was a Japanese GP very much in the Rins-at-Yamaha mould - outmatched badly over one lap, quietly solid in race pace, completely unnoticed.

19th 15th 14th

What fresh twists await us in the final races of the Maverick Vinales/KTM partnership, we shall see, but this was a nicely conventional return.

Vinales wasn't faster than pre-absence but nor was he, really, slower despite the lack of recent mileage - both for muscle mass and in the fact he "doesn't trust" the bike yet.

He was nowhere in qualifying but solid enough in both races, though he did run low on energy at the end thanks to Motegi's physical nature.

22nd 17th 17th

Toprak Razgatlioglu had only done Motegi in a video game before, but seemed to do OK relative to his recent form - even if qualifying is still missing completely.

He also blotted his copybook in the sprint by going off at Turn 1, but remains less bothered by any individual result (a last-lap defeat to Rins in the GP was met with indifference) than by an overall lack of feel on braking.

He says he is "still not riding relaxed", and that this is "the biggest problem".

10th 7th 20th

Just a bit of a mess overall, recovered somewhat with the three points in the sprint. Zarco was fast enough but clearly on too much of a knife edge, as evidenced by the four crashes.

Crash one was while chasing after Alex Marquez on Friday (he was very lucky it didn't cost him Q2), crash two was late on in Q2 because he "wanted too much", crash four was in the grand prix trying to set up a move on Vinales.

But crash three proved most damaging - as Zarco, by his own admission, forgot the rule about re-firing his bike at the side of the track, so was hammered by the stewards for doing so while in the opposite direction to the racing line.

That double long-lap penalty did more damage than any of the incidents.

17th 18th 11th

Brad Binder's Sunday potentially sheds some light on that of his KTM team-mate Acosta - as he and his crew also missed the mark with this hard rear tyre. He said they "toned everything down a few steps" on the set-up trying to protect the centre of the tyre, but instead just blunted his performance to little gain - as "I think we could have done three race distances on it".

So the race was under-par, and the weekend before it likewise, Binder optimistic about going through in Q1 after Friday but crashing instead (which physically limited him for the rest of the weekend) and falling again in the sprint.

20th 16th 19th

This was another weekend that Miller found really, really frustrating, the tone set by a Q1 "f**k-up" that denied him a shot at a more representative grid position.

He was one of two riders running the medium rear in the sprint - Bezzecchi's was mostly fine, but his ended up with "blisters all over".

But that was still the better race of his two. He was left very irritated by what he believed was an overly-conservative approach from his crew to setting tyre pressures - and was in serious trouble, suffering "moment after moment after moment" and then crashing (and remounting), after which he claimed the rear tyre actually cooled down and was nicer to ride.

14th 12th 15th

Franco Morbidelli was surprisingly peppy after the grand prix, which feels out of step with the end result combined with his pedigree and accomplishments as a rider - but there's only so much energy he can expend on this go-nowhere season, and I can accept that.

A deficit of 35 seconds to the winner without the same mitigation that his VR46 team-mate Di Giannantonio had in terms of injury is brutal, and the rest of the weekend was a bit better than that (particularly Q1) but not much better.

5th DNF DNF

This was one of Marquez's best weekends of the year up to Saturday afternoon, and easily his worst from there on.

I believe there's not insignificant mitigation to his role in the multi-bike crash on Saturday, as it seemed he wasn't coming in crazy hot - and was just caught out by Acosta cutting back after being overtaken by Bastianini.

But it was still an error, and Sunday - already compromised by the double long-lap - was very poor in execution, too, from the crash in the warm-up to the sudden exit from eighth in the race caused by an accidental upshift.

items.title: F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz
items.content: <article>F1 "needs to have a hard look at" itself in the wake of unprecedented software glitches that affected the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Carlos Sainz says.</article>

items.title: Podcast: Should F1 have avoided its Malaysia farce?
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
On the latest episode of The Race F1 Podcast, Edd Straw is joined by Jon Noble and Scott Mitchell-Malm to discuss the Malaysia-hosted Bahrain Grand Prix.

It was a race that'll be remembered for Max Verstappen taking his and Red Bull’s first victory of 2026, but it was also one marred by chaos at the first attempt to start it. So what caused the farcical scenes that played out?

That's the key question tackled in part one of the podcast, before Edd, Jon and Scott explain Verstappen and Red Bull's supreme - and somewhat shock - pace this weekend, ask whether Ferrari's tyre blunder cost Lewis Hamilton a shot at victory, and unpack all of the race's other big talking points.

items.title: Edd Straw's 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia F1 driver rankings
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
Wet weather, tyre choices, software bugs and safety cars all added up to Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia chaos at Sepang.

That makes assessing each individual drivers' performance even more critical versus the circumstances facing them, to get a better picture of who excelled - and who didn't - amid the furore.

Here's Edd Straw's final verdict on the field in Sepang:

1st · 1st

Pole position never looked in doubt, topping Q1 and Q2 then delivering two laps good enough to head Q3 with a final advantage of 0.3s.

Losing the lead at the start, primarily down to the Red Bull's trickiness off the line that meant "the engine just completely died", was the only negative of a superbly executed race in which he carved his way to the front well, made the most of the right strategy and didn't put a foot wrong.

The emphatic pace advantage over Hadjar showed that, while the RB22 was performing well, Verstappen was also extracting everything from it with his confidence in attacking the braking zones and corner entries in qualifying particularly standing out.

Pole position and victory never looked in doubt.

2nd · 3rd

Delivered the best-possible result for Ferrari in qualifying with second on the grid, and repeated that trick in the race once you factored in the early losses to taking the race-start proper on slicks.

Had a pace advantage over Leclerc throughout Saturday and Sunday.

While his recovery in the race was assisted by circumstances, he had the pace to make the most of it and would surely have been second - and a potential threat to Verstappen - with a straightforward race.

Fast and pulled off a strong recovery drive that showed his pace.

12th · 8th

With the Aston Martin-Honda package performing well, Alonso made the most of it in qualifying to put himself well up in Q2, which he described as a "miracle".

Taking the start proper on slicks meant he was in an unpromising position, but he showed consistently good pace, including on the hards, to recover to a points finish.

Drove intelligently in the post-safety-car sprint to the flag to take eighth, holding off Lando Norris's McLaren.

For once had a modestly competitive Aston Martin and showed what he can do.

11th · 7th

Top of those who exited after Q2, even with a tow from Lindblad, was a decent performance and, given the disorder in the early part of the race, Lawson deserves credit for having an iron grip on the midfield-leading slot throughout.

Although he ran as high as fourth, the cars he finished behind were all significantly quicker, meaning realistically he achieved the best-possible result.

Got the most out of tricky weekend for Racing Bulls.

3rd · 2nd

The small error at Turn 6 that led to his laptime being deleted, forcing an extra run and limiting him to one set of softs for Q3, potentially cost him a front-row shot given his compromised runplan.

While the Mercedes didn't have the pace to threaten Verstappen, any vague hope Antonelli had of closing the gap after passing Russell vanished when he had his wide moment at the final corner and ended up taking a bite of the pit entry road.

Conclusively the faster Mercedes driver, and emerged with what was probably the best-possible result in the race - although he did have a spell behind Russell after being passed after his unsuccessful defence of the lead against Verstappen.

Another weekend where he was fast and got a good result, but had a few rough edges.

6th · 6th

The comparison with his team-mate is complicated by Norris's straightline speed disadvantage team principal Andrea Stella couldn't explain but characterised as "possibly between one and two tenths of a second" after qualifying.

Didn't maximise what was possible in qualifying, ending up five-thousandths behind Norris after an untidy Turn 2 on his second run meant he had to rely on his first-run time.

Had a decent Sunday, describing it as "a hell of a lot to finish in the same place I started" and produced a strong spell on the hard Pirellis in particular on his way to a result that was probably about right for the car.

Final Q3 run was the only notable negative on a good weekend.

21st · 13th

Given he already had a five-place grid penalty, Alpine opted to take new power unit components that were always going to be required at some point, which locked Colapinto into starting on the back row.

Although Colapinto's practice running was biased more towards race preparation, he showed he had good underlying speed in Q1 by matching Pierre Gasly's time.

Colapinto's race pace was good, but he had one of those races where he was often on the wrong side of strategy decisions - starting on slicks, pitting just before the VSC was deployed for his third stop - which meant he was unable to recover to the points.

Stronger than the on-paper results suggest.

13th · 17th

Sainz was delighted with his qualifying performance on a track that didn't play to the strengths of the Williams.

Ran in the points and as high as sixth early on, but while the car wouldn't have had the pace to stay there his slide was hastened by being understeered into by Gabriel Bortoleto and spinning.

Was never going to finish in the points, but was denied being perhaps five places higher by the Bortoleto collision.

Showed good speed, crucially without repeating any of his recent errors.

22nd · 10th

Carried a back-of-the-grid penalty into the weekend, so his mission in qualifying was primarily to reach Q2 then be used to provide a tow for Lawson, which he did well.

Recovered from starting at the back thanks to taking the start proper on inters, a team call, and was in contention for a minor points position throughout, although didn't always appear to be on top of the tyre management.

Outwitted Nico Hulkenberg in their late battle to secure the final point.

Salvaged a point from unpromising circumstances.

7th · 20th

Never looked to have the pace to match Antonelli in qualifying, which was proved by the 0.240s Q3 deficit despite having two runs compared to his team-mate's one.

Capitalised on Antonelli's fight with Verstappen to pass his team-mate with a well-executed move, although he didn't have the pace to hold onto it.

The power unit problem that cost third place late on was entirely out of his hands.

Unlucky in the race but a step behind Antonelli all weekend.

20th · 19th

Perez's weekend can only be evaluated within the context of him running not only the old-specification Ferrari ADUO 1 power unit, but also it being a tired one that didn't even give its optimum performance.

Allowing for the power unit disadvantage, Perez's pace stacked up well against Bottas when you adjust for that.

The Cadillac was the slowest car by some margin, so it's no surprise Perez finished last.

Considering the ageing power unit, a good weekend.

8th · 5th

Had a consistent pace deficit to Verstappen, with the 0.428s gap in qualifying representative.

Although he had a five-place grid penalty for taking a new ICE, Hadjar ran fourth in the first stint but never showed anything like the pace of Verstappen - struggling for grip throughout, and having a formation-lap off for good measure.

While team principal Laurent Mekies obliquely referred to the fact that "not everything went well with his car", there was no clear explanation for the lack of pace - although slipping from third at the final safety-car restart to fifth behind the two Ferraris was attributed by Hadjar to the battery being lower on energy than it needed to be.

A solid result on paper, but was not at anything like Verstappen's level all weekend.

14th · 12th

Matched Alonso in Q1, but couldn't go with him in Q2 and ended up 0.346s slower.

After switching from slicks to intermediates for the start proper, made some progress but struggled with his second hard stint and lost ground.

Ultimately, didn't quite have the same all-round pace as Alonso (although there were encouraging patches) and couldn't quite force himself into the points battle.

Had a reasonable weekend in a car that at least gave him something to race for.

16th · 14th

What was characterised as a set-up error - described as an "operational" mistake by the team - that ruined FP2 put him on the back foot heading into Saturday.

Eliminated in Q1 after finally finding a good balance for the final run, which was enough to beat Ocon by a quarter of a second.

Slicks for the start put Bearman on the back foot and, given the car pace, it's no surprise he never ran higher than 13th - with the timing of the VSC allowing him to finish ahead of Ocon.

Did a decent job considering the Friday problem and race circumstances.

17th · 15th

While elimination in Q1 was no great surprise, Ocon ended up behind Bearman having been the first driver to complete his last lap on a rapidly-improving track surface.

Thrust himself into points contention with a good first racing lap and the right call to use intermediates.

Spent much of the race trying to defy competitive gravity, but a combination of pushing too hard once he switched to hards, running wide in the pit-entry road prior to a slightly slow stop, and a green-flag pit stop when others hit the VSC that was deployed shortly afterwards, added up to 15th place.

At least kept the uncompetitive Haas in the points mix for some of the race.

15th · 11th

While Hulkenberg's underlying pace meant he might have had a shot at joining Bortoleto in Q3, a mistake on his final Q1 lap meant he was eliminated.

Pitted before the start proper to bail out of starting on softs before becoming the first to choose to switch back to slicks.

Was in the mix for points, but lost out late on to Lindblad.

Fell short of the points finish that was on offer.

18th · DNF

Complained throughout the weekend about not having optimum parts available.Made an error on his last Q1 run, which cost any chance of joining Sainz in Q2.

Although he ran seventh early on, Albon's race was troubled even before he retired with a gearbox problem - thanks to a short stint after flatspotting the softs and brake struggles.

There were clearly problems, but also a few errors.

4th · 4th

Qualifying gradually slipped away from him as it progressed thanks to what he called an "aggressive" set-up choice that meant he was struggling badly with rear-tyre overheating.

Locked up and clipped the back of Hulkenberg's Audi on the first racing lap, forcing a pitstop for a new nose. While being on slicks was a mitigating factor, he was aware grip was low.

Recovered well in the race, albeit with the help of circumstances, but struggled for balance, likely as a carryover from the set-up decisions made before qualifying.

Didn't get the best out of the car and made a significant early-race error.

10th · 18th

Did a superb job in qualifying to make Q3, although the pace was probably not in the car to have beaten Gasly.

Pitted for intermediates after initially intending to take the start proper on softs, but a misjudgement in low-grip conditions while battling with Sainz that led to him understeering into the Williams meant he had to pit for a new nose and was hit with a 10-second penalty.

Floor damage from the impact meant the rest of his race was compromised.

Qualifying was superb, but early-race mistake ruined his chances.

9th · 16th

Made the most of the Alpine in qualifying, comfortably leading the midfield and putting the car in the highest possible starting position.

Threw away ninth place and lost places to an off on slicks while attempting to warm the tyres prior to the start proper, although that likely just hastened his drop back.

Never recovered from the early losses and ended up not helped by a green-flag pitstop when others were able to stop under VSC, making this race a missed opportunity.

Strong in qualifying, but off before the start proper set the negative trajectory.

5th · 9th

Qualified as well as he could have done, especially considering a straightline deficit rated by the team as 0.1-0.2s compared to Piastri.

The error under the safety car when he had to run into the gravel at Turn 1 in avoidance of the cars ahead - including Piastri - was a needless one for a driver of his experience.

Although he recovered to ninth having dropped to 11th with his mistake, after picking off Lindblad and Hulkenberg, he never managed to mount a serious attack on Alonso in the brief chase at the end of the race.

Although his pace was good, the safety-car off tanks his rating given it was an amateur mistake.

19th · DNF

Ran the Ferrari ADUO 2 power unit for the first time, which locked in a car-performance advantage over Perez for the weekend.

Felt he extracted the maximum from the car in Q1, although his pace advantage over Perez was down to speed on the straights.

Had a dismal race, accepting responsibility for the choice to start on slicks (although he was far from the only one) but spinning into the gravel on lap eight.

Early-race spin into retirement turned a solid weekend into a bad one.

How do the rankings work?

The 22 drivers are ranked in order of performance from best to worst on each grand prix weekend. This will be based on the full range of criteria, ranging from pace and racecraft to consistency and whether they made key mistakes. How close each driver got to delivering on the maximum performance potential of the car will be an essential consideration.

It’s important to note both that this reflects performance across the entire weekend, cognisant of the fact that qualifying is effectively ‘lap 0’ of the race and key to laying the foundations to the race, and that it is not a ranking of the all-round qualities of each driver. It’s simply about how they performed on a given weekend. Therefore, the ranking will fluctuate significantly from weekend to weekend.

And with each of the 11 cars fundamentally having different performance potential and ‘luck’ (i.e. factors outside of a driver’s control) contributing to the way the weekend plays out, this ranking will also differ significantly from the overall results.

items.title: Can anyone challenge world champion Marlen Reusser? – European Championship elite women's time trial contenders
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The European Championships have only included elite races since 2016, and in those 10 editions just four riders have held the women's time trial title, with Ellen van Dijk, Marlen Reusser, Anna van der Breggen and Lotte Kopecky all tasting success. Will there be a new name in 2026? Or will Marlen Reusser set a new record of five titles, to go with her second world title won in Montreal two weeks ago?

This year’s race starts and finishes in the central Slovenian town of Šenčur, and whoever takes the title this year will need to overcome a challenging 22.1km course which includes almost 400m of vertical ascent, almost all of which comes in the first half of the race.

The main challenge comes in the form of the climb to Možjanca, which averages 10.2% gradient over its 2km and tops out a third of the way through the course. Though there are steeper ramps at the top, it’s a fairly steady gradient which will suit the TT specialists who can set a strong rhythm.

While there are narrow sections and some turns, it is not a technical route, though there is a tight hairpin turn on the descent where the road surface appears fairly poor, so riders will need to be concentrated to get through that unscathed. After that, the final kilometres are almost entirely flat, and while it’s a different type of course, it’s hard to look past those who performed well at the Montreal World Championships. Here are our contenders for the stars and stripes skinsuit.

After her dominant ride at the World Championships in Montreal, Switzerland’s Marlen Reusser will start as the outright favourite for another title. While her palmarès indicates she is far more than a pure time trial specialist, she is currently the most accomplished woman against the clock and bang in form, finishing third in the Euros road race over the weekend.

What’s more, the course suits her, though others may be better than her on the early steep climb, once over that, expect the Swiss superstar to build her advantage.

The one note of caution is her performance on the mountain time trial of this year’s Giro d’Italia Women when she finished well behind winner, Anna van der Breggen, though the Dutchwoman is absent from this year's European Championships.

Maybe another motivation for Reusser is her place in history. Should she take a fifth title on Wednesday, she will hold the record for European titles, surpassing Ellen van Dijk’s four victories, which she equalled last year.

Winning the Euros road race on Saturday, Demi Vollering might be the best all-round rider in the women’s peloton at the moment, but she’s not won a time trial since the 2024 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, and only managed eighth place in the recent World Championships.

The Slovenian course suits her more than that in Canada, though, the steep, early climb will almost certainly allow her to gain time on all her rivals, though she will then need to hold on to her advantage for the rest of the course.

She might not be a regular winner against the clock, but she is almost always there or thereabouts and clearly in form right now, winning both Worlds and Europeans road races. Combine that ability with a course which suits her and a voracious appetite for success, and no one would be surprised if she takes another victory on Wednesday.

After finishing just outside the medals in the Montreal individual time trial, Elisa Longo Borghini won the mixed team relay before taking third in the road race, so it’s clear the Italian has struck a rich vein of form.

After missing much of the spring with illness, she has been improving since returning to health, and we should expect her to make the podium on Wednesday. Longo Borghini is arguably a better climber than Reusser, and she’s certainly a better descender, so if she can take time on the Swiss rider on the climb, she should be able to consolidate that on the descent.

However, in contrast to the prolific Reusser, she has only ever won two time trials outside the Italian Championships, the most recent of which was two years ago, 10 years after the other. However, like Vollering she is always there or thereabouts, and a top result is likely.

Fifth in Montreal, Cédrine Kerbaol is another rider in fine form to take on Europeans this week. At 25-years-old she is still improving every year and, as one of the peloton’s preeminent climbers we can expect her to deal with the early gradients well.

Like Longo Borghini, she’s also a brilliant descender, so may well be able to take time on the descent, and her performance in Canada is proof she can deal with the flat run-in well enough to make the podium.

Though she was only the second-best German rider in the World Championships last week, taking seventh place, just over a minute behind compatriot Franziska Koch, Antonia Niedermaier is by far the better climber of the pair and will be able to gain time in those challenging early kilometres.

The 23-year-old took fourth place in the Giro d’Italia’s mountain time trial in May, just 15 seconds behind Reusser, and though this is less challenging terrain than that, Niedermaier can be expected to put in a good performance in Slovenia this week.

While she may not be the climber her compatriot Niedermaier is, Franziska Koch has proved this year that there is almost nothing she cannot do. Since arriving at FDJ United-Suez she has improved exponentially, and her TT bronze medal in Montreal shows just how good she is against the clock.

While her climbing is much better than before, the day’s ascent will prove a major obstacle to success for Koch, though there is every chance she can make up time on the descent and flatter parts of the course.

This year’s Polish time trial champion, Dominika Włodarczyk, is much improved against the clock this season, with her ninth place at the Worlds a best-ever result. Only 25, she has always been good at the discipline, bagging some decent results as a junior, it’s just taken her time to become competitive in the elite ranks.

What’s more, she has established herself as an excellent climber, finishing eighth on the Mont Ventoux stage of the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift this year and finishing seventh overall, so the Možjanca climb will be well within her talents.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney will also race the TT for Poland, and whilst the time trial was once considered one of her weaknesses, she put in a hugely improved ride against the clock at the Tour de France earlier this summer, so don't write her off entirely.

  • – Put in a decent ride in Montreal but will be hindered by the climb
  • Juliette Berthet (France) – Will look to come back from an unusually sub-par performance at Worlds
  • –reat against the clock but unlikely to challenge the very best for a medal
  • Lauren Dickson (Great Britain) – Sixth on the Giro mountain TT, but still developing as a time trialist

UAE Team L'IMAD shutter development squad amid ongoing turbulence
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
UAE Team L'IMAD are closing their development squad at end of 2026, they announced on Monday, but they have vowed to continue supporting the riders through 2027.

The UAE Development Team was set up in 2023 as a women's Continental team, and has seen riders like Paula Blasi, Lara Gillespie and Linda Zanetti pass through its ranks, all of whom are now successful WorldTour riders.

However, despite taking multiple wins in 2026, the separate development programme will soon be closing down, with the team integrating its development mission into the WorldTour team. This year, the UAE Development Team has 11 riders on its roster, though only one – Abigail Miller – officially had a contract for 2027.

"UAE Team L’IMAD has confirmed that the UAE Development Team will not continue as a separate UCI Women’s Continental Team for the 2027 season. Following a review of its sporting organisation, the team is changing how it supports the development of young riders," a statement from the team read.

"Within its WorldTour structure, UAE Team L’IMAD will continue to develop young riders who are ready to take that step. They will have the opportunity to learn alongside experienced teammates, with their progression guided by individual readiness and racing opportunities suited to their development."

The statement also stated that the current riders will continue to be supported by the team in 2027 "with support tailored to their individual needs and stage of development", adding that "the priority is to help each athlete continue progressing in her career".

With 11 riders on the team this year, though, it's unclear what that support will look like – not all of them can be promoted to the WorldTour team, so the majority of riders will have to find a new team if they wish to continue racing on the road in 2027, even with UAE support.

The landscape of women's development teams

Whilst almost all men's WorldTour teams now have U23 development squads, it is still a rarer concept in women's cycling, where there is no dedicated U23 racing circuit. In 2026, AG Insurance-Soudal, Canyon-SRAM, Liv AlUla Jayco, UAE and Fenix-Premier Tech all have development teams, but that list will drop to just four in 2027.

Whilst plenty of teams opt to integrate their development efforts within their main WorldTour squad, or by partnering with an existing Continental team, the benefit of having a specific development squad is that it gives teams many more roster spots for young riders, and the ability to run a dual programme.

Despite losing those extra spots, and therefore unavoidably narrowing the scope of their development programme, UAE affirmed that helping riders progress is still a core part of the team's ethos.

"We are proud of what our Development Team has achieved and grateful to everyone who has contributed. Our priority now is to support our riders through this change and help them continue progressing," team president Melissa Moncada said.

"Developing young talent remains part of our commitment to women’s cycling. We want every young rider in our WorldTour team to have the time, guidance and opportunities she needs to grow.”

Turbulent times at UAE Team L'IMAD

The closure of UAE's development team is not only unfortunate news for their current roster and the women's development circuit in general, but it is also another big change in what has been a turbulent summer for UAE Team L'IMAD.

They are going through a significant management restructuring, with team CEO Yana Seel exiting the team in August, and no permanent replacement in post yet. Senior DS Cherie Pridham was touted as a possible successor, but the Brit is also leaving the team for Human Powered Health, along with multiple other sports directors – over half the current DS line-up is departing at the end of 2026.

Sponsored by a UAE sovereign wealth fund and widely understood to have one of the largest budgets in the women's peloton, money does not seem to be the issue at UAE Team L'IMAD, but rather questions and concerns over management and stability behind the scenes.

At WorldTour level, the team has made two new signings for 2027 so far – Pfeiffer Georgi from Picnic PostNL and Lily Williams from Human Powered Health – and will still have riders like Elisa Longo Borghini and Mavi García on their books next season, so there is no question over their survival or strength, just the shape and future of the management behind the team.

items.title: Gary Anderson: F1 got lucky Malaysia chaos wasn't worse
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
When the Formula 1 cars headed off on their formation lap for the Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang, I didn't know whether to laugh or cry.

I simply couldn't believe what I was seeing and felt that a few million other people and I were just about to be robbed of what should have turned out to be a great race. Old sparring partners Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton sitting side by side on the front row was going to be epic.

The weather conditions changing at the last minute always spices things up, but cars were basically stopping everywhere.

It was all through no fault of the drivers or the teams; their hands are tied with these stupid 2026 regulations.

I'm just about fed up with complaining about them. They are so far away from what I would call racing or what a racing driver wants that it just makes a mockery of what is supposed to be the crème de la crème of motorsport.

I'm not going to go into the fact that these cars can't or aren't allowed even to venture out on the track in the wet - that's all for another day!

Today's gripe is simply about how these stupid power unit regulations and how they are implemented are basically dangerous.

How many times this year, after seeing a driver make what we thought was an error, does that driver come on the radio and say ‘I have no idea what just happened there'? We only have to go back to Baku when Valtteri Bottas went into the safety barrier on the final lap of the race. This happened because he went down the escape road at Turn 1, the car “got confused” about where it was on the track, so instead of slowing down when he pressed the brake pedal as he wanted to, it went straight on into the barriers.

If we look at the sporting regulations; Article B1.8.1 states: “The driver must drive the F1 car alone and unaided.”

Now I completely understand why the paddle-shift gear-change system complies with that requirement, as the driver has to instigate the gear change by operating the paddle. However, I am confused that if the driver is pressing the brake pedal and the car ‘decides' it doesn't want to slow down, how does that comply with Article B1.8.1?

Moving that onto what happened on the formation lap for the Bahrain GP, we have the following rules being severely tested;

Article B1.8.5 states: “At no time may an F1 car be driven unnecessarily slowly, erratically or in a manner which could be deemed potentially dangerous to other drivers or any other person.”

And Article B1.8.7 states ”Any driver whose car has a significant failure or fault which means it cannot reasonably return to the pitlane without unnecessarily impeding another competitor or otherwise hindering the competition must leave the track as soon as it is safe to do so.”

In the technical regulations, Article C1.4 states: “The stewards may prohibit the participation of a vehicle whose construction is deemed to be dangerous.

“Should the relevant information become apparent during a session, such a decision may apply with immediate effect.”

And Article C1.5 states: “F1 cars must comply with these regulations in their entirety at all times during a competition,” and Article C1.7 says “It is the duty of each competitor to satisfy the FIA and the stewards that its Formula 1 car complies with these regulations in their entirety at all times during a competition.

“With regard to power units used on a Formula 1 car, this duty and responsibility also extends to the PU manufacturer.”

If you sum those up, the driver, the teams and the power unit manufacturer's hands are tied by an inadequate understanding and, from that lack of understanding, an inadequate set of regulations.

If we just take the startline chaos we saw in pre-season testing, where the cars couldn't manage a practice start, the FIA changed the start procedure to incorporate a five-second turbo spool-up time prior to the lights coming on. This was because of the lack of understanding of how much the teams would struggle after the removal of the MGU-H.

Being the governing body, the FIA could change that and any regulation it wanted by deeming it as a safety change. Stranded cars on the grid are dangerous but it never needed to get to that point in the first place.

And back to these power units as they are now, how long do we have to wait before someone gets hurt? Just imagine the chaos that was just around the corner if the race at Sepang had actually started in dry conditions and that thunderstorm came in around lap five.

We would have had cars littered all around the track with the drivers playing with the steering wheel buttons a bit like Elton John on his piano keys; the only difference would be they would be hitting control-alt-delete.

While they were doing that, they wouldn't have been complying with either the no erratic driving rule of Article B1.8.5 or the don't unnecessarily impede others with an ailing car mentioned in Article B1.8.7.

I'm not going to go into the rights and wrongs of what happened at Sepang because, in reality, it doesn't really matter what the details of the reason it happened were. It shouldn't have happened.

However, what worries me more is that the regulation setter, the FIA, was able to come up with a software fix in a very short amount of time and install it in all cars without any depth of real-world testing. Then what other software gremlins are lurking in there, waiting to rear their ugly head?

Now's the time to act with maturity and responsibility and react to the situation we saw at Sepang. Yes the FIA say it covered that problem with a software fix, but did it fully eradicate it or is the next problem lurking just around the corner?

This was race 16 of this season. Yes, it was the first wet event, but even still, the problems we have should not be happening.

I have been saying for a long time that the driver needs to be given control of the car through their two pedals and the steering wheel. Pull or push the upshift paddle for an upshift, pull or push the downshift paddle for a downshift, turn it to the left if you want to go left, turn it to the right if you want to go right, press the brake pedal if you want to slow down; the harder you press, the more you slow; press the torque (throttle) pedal if you want to go faster; the further you press it, the more torque you get.

As far as the harvesting and deployment is concerned it is very easy to fix. You need to put the cart before the horse instead of someone inventing this 50/50% internal combustion engine to electrical torque usage. And that 50/50 split is - other than for a very short snapshot in time per lap - basically impossible when you have cars that over an average lap are requesting positive torque from say 20% through to 100% (with this the driver is basically saying ‘I want to go faster') for roughly 60% of the lap with a negative torque request (I.e. less than 10% positive torque and brake pressure) from say 20% to 100% of the maximum brake pressure seen on a lap (the driver is basically saying ‘I want to go slower') of the brake pressure for only 20% of a lap.

If you simply take those numbers you get 80% of the lap either accelerating or braking significantly, the other 20% is down to part throttle usage. If they are anywhere near correct then you either need three times the harvesting capability you have relative to deployment, or you go to a 75% internal combustion engine and a 25% electrical torque balance.

Yes, it will mean that this mythical 1000bhp and speeds in excess of 350km/h (218mph) on the straights that F1 seems to be chasing will be reduced to probably 850bhp and 320km/h (199mph), but do we really care? I remember when that 200mph in old money was seen as a great threshold to shoot at. This ratio could be optimised pre-event for each circuit by simply averaging out the balance request from the five power unit manufacturers.

After everything settled down, we still had a very good race, but we need to remember that one of the cars that stopped on that initial formation lap was Hamilton, before his Ferrari eventually restarted. After a dubious tyre choice of slicks for the restart, which basically left him over a minute behind the leader, with a little help from the VSC and then the safety car, he ended up on the podium. However, through no fault of his own or his team, his Ferrari could have ended up not even starting.

items.title: Key figure in Honda's F1 return to be replaced in 2027
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Honda will get a new racing boss next year after the retirement of current president and CEO Koji Watanabe, who helped manage the manufacturer’s official return to Formula 1.

Watanabe will be replaced as the head of Honda Racing Corporation by Keiichi Yasuda on January 1, slightly earlier than executive-level changes would typically happen in April to align with the motorsport season.

Yasuda is currently HRC’s executive vice president and representative director.

Like Watanabe, he is a company man who has been with Honda since 1990. Prior to his HRC leadership role, which included overseeing Honda’s official F1 return under the new 2026 engine regulations, Watanabe rose to be a senior figure on the communications and marketing side within Honda.

He assumed the HRC job as part of Honda’s restructuring of its motorsport efforts in 2022 when it unified its motorcycle and car racing programmes under the same entity.

That made Watanabe a senior figure and spokesperson for Honda’s enduring relationship with Red Bull to the end of 2025 and then its new engine project with Aston Martin this year.

Honda has had a dismal formal return to F1, though, suffering a lack of performance even since the chronic reliability problems that caused an embarrassing start to the season across testing and the early races.

This has at least in part been caused by Honda’s shaky commitment to F1 and its damaging decision to withdraw officially at the end of 2021 - only continuing as effectively a service partner to Red Bull, managing the engines that were frozen in homologation from 2022 to 2025.

Honda’s board then decided to re-commit to F1 for the new rules in 2026 after all, which meant attempting to revive a project that had been gutted to redistribute engineers to other programmes - thus leaving Honda on the back foot for the new regulations.

One of the consequences of this was Aston Martin claiming it only discovered late last year just how different the Honda project was to its previous, more successful era with Red Bull.

The key decision for this was made before Watanabe was put in charge of HRC, though his role inevitably made him an important figure thereafter even if his influence over the state of the project this year is hard to discern.

Honda says the change for 2027 is being made “as part of a planned periodic personnel rotation designed to strengthen the management structure in response to global transformation and to accelerate business expansion for the next generation”.

Yasuda comes from the human resources side of Honda, with an interest in its motorcycle activities, and rose to the top position in Honda's HR division prior to joining HRC in 2026.

items.title: What’s behind Marquez becoming so serious
Most aero socks are a waste of money: Here's the wind tunnel verified proof
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
Even though aerodynamics has become priority number one for most competitive cyclists buying new kit, aero socks are perhaps the most ridiculed upgrade of the past decade.

Speaking generally, the promise of 'free' (albeit often very expensive) speed is hard to ignore, compounded by the fact that pro cyclists – who rarely need to worry about the accompanying expense – place extreme importance on the matter as their careers can be made or lost by it.

Yet while most aero products are embraced quickly and without second thought, aero socks took a good while to gain acceptance. They didn't pass the fashion test, and the old guard dismissed them as a gimmick or a marginal gain too far. But when comparative tests started showing measurable benefits, more and more teams started wearing them, and nowadays, they're a staple in the pro peloton. You'll spot amateurs in them too, especially on race day.

We've now hit a point where some aero socks are so highly technical and researched that they regularly fetch up to £50+ per pair, and some even stretch as far as £100, and that's before we get into custom territory. The thing is, others can be had for just £3 if you know where to shop.

So do you actually stand to save more watts by buying the more expensive - or name brand - socks?

To find out, we collated 26 pairs of socks and headed to the wind tunnel.

Our cohort included 22 pairs from named cycling brands, including Velotoze, Rule28, Aero Cycling Gear, NoPinz, Rapha, Castelli, Assos and more.

It also included a pair of comparatively cheap 'Rock Bros' socks that we bought from Amazon, an extremely cheap pair of 'West Biking' socks from Temu, a pair of cotton everyday socks from the British high-street clothing store Next, as well as some technical hiking socks from another high-street store.

The full list, in alphabetical order, is as follows:

  • Aero Cycling gear v5 Hexaflow
  • Mountain Warehouse Hiking Socks
  • Next everyday cotton socks
  • Rule 28 Neo Aero Sock (Double Layer)

So are expensive aero socks any faster than cheap aero socks? Does a pair of aero socks beat a pair of nominally 'standard' cycling socks? What about compared to a pair of everyday or hiking socks?

The title of this article has probably already given you a clue as to the answers to some of these questions, but scroll down to find out the details.

Unlike previous CN Labs tests, where you're forced to read through (or scroll past) 3000 words explaining the protocols, caveats and standardisations, I'm going to dive straight into the results and do the nerdy stuff later. Please do take time to read the nerdy bits below, though, as that'll help you understand how we landed on the data and what caveats apply.

It's also important to state up front that the data is subject to an error margin of 0.2w at the lower speed, and 1.17w at the higher speed.

The biggest thing of note here is that there are very small differences between all the pairs of aero socks on test. There's just 1.85 watts between the fastest and slowest, and the difference between many of the socks in between is smaller than our error margin.

The Aero Cycling Gear V5 was fastest, but both NoPinz's Sonic and Rule 28's One Aero Sock can lay claim to victory too, with the error margin taken into account.

According to Rule 28, its more expensive Neo Aero Sock, with its double-layer finish, was designed for speeds over 55km/h for time trialling and track riding, so its mid-table result isn't a surprise here. It's also a lesson in choosing the right product for your needs, as spending more money doesn't automatically equal better performance across the board.

Just off the podium, the NoPinz Hypersonic Mk2, Sockeloen FSOTP 468 and Santini Madss are close behind, with Castelli's Fast Feet 4 sitting just behind those.

And then the next dozen are all pretty much indistinguishable, despite the price bracket ranging from £3.68 for the 'West Biking' brand of socks we bought from Temu, to £50 for the Rapha and Assos options.

Behind this, there are small steps down, before a bigger jump to the two pairs of non-cycling socks.

The error margin here is around 50% bigger than that of the 30km/h test, meaning even more potential for crossover between results. The results show that the Rule 28 One Aero Sock banked the best result, but it was a bit of a lottery as to which actually came out on top. Any of the top 17 - yes, seventeen - can claim the top spot, because they were all within 1.17 watts (our error margin) of the winner.

And to clarify, this is a pretty tight error margin at such a high speed, just ten counts (or 0.0010) in terms of CdA. So while it looks like we've just performed a bad test that shows all socks as being about the same, that's because all the socks are… about the same.

When you get into the bottom third of the table, we do start to see some differences, but most of those still sit within the error margin of five places either above or below.

Notably, the Velotoze Aero Pro is a step behind the others, despite being a high-priced aero product. Having shared the data with Velotoze, we're at a loss as to what caused this. It could be that the material was overstretched when fitted, or it could have been a glitch. It doesn't concur with Velotoze's own data, which showed them to be 6 watts faster than Velotoze' baseline coolmax socks at 40km/h in its own internal testing.

And the Veto 1.0 is a standard cycling sock by design, with none of your typical aero fabrics or trip strips, nor the common papery thin fragility, but the brand does claim to have tested them in a wind tunnel with good results.

We're looking at a gap of 4.9 watts (+/- 1.17w) between the fastest and slowest cycling socks on test, which is still better than a kick in the teeth, but given the £14.99 pair of Rock Bros socks from Amazon are just as fast as the £30-50 pairs from all the big brands, it's a damning outcome for anyone charging big money promising aero gains.

And like the 30km/h data above, the distant duo at the bottom of the table (in the form of the hiking socks and the everyday cotton socks) are the exception that proves the rule. There's a further five watts between the slowest aero socks and the slowest non-cycling socks.

I guess my main regret here is not taking more 'normal' cycling socks along to see how they compare, but I'm quite confident they'd sit within the error margin too.

While there's no clear trend that we can see, it's interesting to see how the order differs at the two speeds.

The consistent position of the two non-cycling socks – the hiking socks and the cotton everyday socks – at the bottom of the table is reassurance that the wind tunnel was spitting out accurate numbers. If a pair of woolly socks from my local hiking store outperformed dedicated aero socks, I'd be concerned we'd done something wrong.

While it's fair to say the difference between each pair of socks is minimal, can we at least spot a trend with taller generally being faster than shorter?

That's long been the general train of thought. It's why we see time triallists in knee-high socks, and partly why the UCI banned socks over a certain height (although that was mainly because they look weird too).

To find out, I've grouped the socks by their height to see if taller does indeed equal faster.

There's a slight bias towards better performance at the taller heights, but it's far from clearcut. We had socks here ranging from 20cm to 26cm tall, but some of the socks in the 20cm category are just as fast as those up at 24 and 26cm.

This one's so clear-cut that it doesn't even need a graph to prove it. The £3 socks are mid-table, the £14.99 socks are on the podium, and more than one near-£50 pair sits in the bottom third of our test.

There's no clear correlation between price and aerodynamic performance.

On the day, we decided that next time, we'd try to work with a brand like Sockeloen or Vorteq to create a custom-fitted pair to see if that makes any difference. Sockeloen offers a €1000 option that involves aero consultancy, for example.

Of course, cheaper items - socks and otherwise - could cut corners in other areas. They might be faster in a one-minute wind tunnel test, but if they lose their stick and fall down halfway through a ride, or if they lose their stretch and become baggy after three washes, or they fall apart entirely, you're giving away all the aero gains and more.

The contrary to that, though, is that many aero socks from big-name brands are incredibly fragile. Some are much better than others, but the papery finish you get on some is easy to damage. I've ripped three pairs in the past year alone. And the lack of stretch in the material on others means you really need to fight to get them on, which in turn increases the risk of damage.

That's not the subject of today's test, so we will be putting the various socks through their real-world paces to see how they fare in longer-term use.

But even so, when there's no aero performance guarantee, and the risk of damage means they could last just as long as something made less well, why buy something at 3x - or, in the case of the Temu socks, 14x - the price?

There are clearly watts to be saved between the non-cycling socks (everyday cotton and the hiking socks) and the cycling socks, of which the best example is the Veto 1.0.

There is then another small uptick to the nominally 'aero' socks, but the difference between that Veto 1.0 and an 'aero' cycling sock could range anywhere from negative three watts (ie, worse) to a maximum of around six watts (both at 45km/h).

But given our data shows small differences between the aero socks, there's no single winner in today's test. Rule 28 will enjoy the results of the 45km/h test, and likewise Aero Cycling Gear in the 30km/h test, but the reality is the socks are all so close to one another that you, as a consumer, should probably just buy the cheapest, or the ones you like the look of most.

At £3.68, the 'West Biking' socks I bought from Temu promise incredible aero performance in terms of watts saved vs money spent. They did feel pretty basic in their materials, though, as can be expected at a price that would allow you to buy FOURTEEN pairs for the same cost as the most expensive on test.

The feel and quality of the £14.99 'Rock Bros Grid' socks from Amazon were just as good as most of the 'big brand' products, though, so I'd be very tempted to buy those; and that's still between half and a third of the price of most others here. The only downside to those is the big 'Rock' on one leg and 'Bros' on the other, but they make them in dozens of various colours and designs. If they made them in pure white, I expect they'd sell incredibly well.

Assuming you do want to buy something that promises to be aero, there's very little way to know which is the best one for you.

There's no obvious correlation between aero performance and cuff height, price, or brand. They're also all designed to work at varying speeds, and the optimal pair for you will probably depend on what sort of riding you're doing, whether it's windy, how many people you're riding with, and the shape and size of your legs.

Therefore, unless you're going to hire a wind tunnel and a team of data scientists to run simulations on your upcoming race, you're probably best off just buying the cheap ones and spending the rest of the money on carbs.

To find out how aerodynamic they were, we took all the socks to the wind tunnel at the Silverstone Sports Engineering Hub.

The wind tunnel measures CdA (Coefficient of Drag x Area), which quantifies how easily something passes through the air. The 'Coefficient of Drag' is a measure of how easily air passes over something's surface, while the 'Area' is a simple measure of its size. Reducing the size of something isn't always possible (although there is a size difference between a hiking sock and a paper-thin aero sock), so helping the air flow over it neatly is where the aerodynamicist's skill comes in, with things like ribbed fabrics and trip strips.

As you'll have seen above, we tested each pair at two wind speeds: 30km/h and 45km/h, to try to see if any of the socks performed better at one speed over the other. We used a powered roller to spin the wheels at the same speed as the wind, to add a little more realism to the test.

We tested each pair of socks on a static-leg mannequin. While a pedalling leg mannequin is more realistic, it's not something we currently have access to. Fortunately, the repeatability of a static leg mannequin is generally better, so we'd have less accuracy and fewer conclusions. The repeatability of a real rider is much lower, and would have led to an error margin approximately 3x the size of what we had.

We tested at three different yaw angles: -5°, 0°, and +5°. This is a narrower sweep than our bike tests, but it still covered the angles that riders will experience a vast majority of the time, and it still allowed us to calculate a single wind-averaged drag figure representative of real-world conditions. We could have stopped at zero degrees – a direct headwind – since most socks are largely symmetrical, but we opted to test both sides to be more confident in the data we were seeing.

Each measurement was captured for 15 seconds. This is approximately twice as long as needed to see a steady CdA figure and get a result that we can confidently call accurate – a mannequin doesn't move, so there's no unwanted wobbles or head tilts that need to be smoothed out by a longer exposure – but shortening the sample time would have only saved us around five minutes across the whole test, so not really worth it. Better to have extra confidence in the data.

Aside from the socks, everything was kept exactly the same for each test. That includes the bike, the mannequin, its position on the bike, its clothing, its helmet, the shoes, and so on.

We didn't standardise the sock height across all socks, because some are designed to be around 20cm tall, whereas others sat at 26cm. Trying to run everything at 23cm would have meant some being overly stretched, and others being baggy and wrinkled.

Instead, we fitted each one in a way that felt natural – not too stretched, but not loose or baggy – and we measured the height (ensuring it was equal on both legs too). Then we adjusted it to the nearest centimetre, so as to standardise socks somewhat against similar-height competitors.

Those heights were then correlated against performance to see if we could spot a trend between height and aero.

To quantify the error margin, we tested the same pair of socks at three points throughout the test and then worked out the maximum gap between them. That difference was then used as the error margin.

That equated to an error margin of 0.2 watts at 30km/h, and was slightly bigger at 45km/h, coming in at 1.17w. Those margins are outlined in the graphs above.

It's important to note that this error margin is around 3x better than the last time we tested aero socks - which was done with a real rider - and resulted in an error margin of over 3 watts. Even so, the error is still big enough to encompass around half the socks we tested, and thus prove that although some are faster than others, the differences are quite minuscule.

As ever, our data is representative of our day of testing and is far from the final word on the aerodynamic performance of these products, especially as it might pertain to each individual using them.

We're proud to say the test is completely impartial, and we believe it is the biggest of its kind in terms of the number of products tested, but we don't pretend it's the be-all and end-all.

We simply hope that it provides an extra stream of comparison data for our readers, to help them choose which one to buy in the broader context of other similar aero comparisons, as well as the various other metrics that govern a good or bad purchase (ie price, comfort, aesthetics, and so on).

With that in mind, there are some unexpected results that are worth highlighting. The Velotoze Pro Aero is perhaps the biggest outlier in the 45km/h test. It doesn't align with the 30km/h test, nor Velotoze's own measurements, and we've been back and forth with them to try to understand it. Theories include possibly overstretching the sock on fitting, but we've been unable to pinpoint an obvious error.

Another includes the Sockeloen FSOTP 468. Despite being designed to excel at 46.8km/h (hence the name), it dropped down the order at the nearby 45km/h speed. This is closer to the others and thus could just be a fault of the error margin, but still it's surprising to see it perform worse than its peers at a speed it was designed to excel at. These socks weren't brand new out of the box; they'd been worn a few times since we received them for our prior aero sock test. They hadn't stretched to any noticeable extent, but my strongest theory here is that they've lost some of their performance in age.

The Assos socks were also used, held over from our previous round of sock testing in 2024, and despite performing really well in our previous test, they were mid-table this time. It's possibly a coincidence, but it could add weight to the above.

When making calculations for speed (and in turn, time to complete a 40km TT), we aren't accounting for gradients, corners, drivetrain loss or any other variable. We're looking for the difference between each product here, not an absolute forecast.

And finally, this test wasn't in any way sponsored. We paid for the wind tunnel hire at the normal rate, and this test, like all of our CN Labs projects, is made possible solely and entirely by the paying subscribers. Without your support, these tests wouldn't happen, so thank you.
