items.title: Preseason Game Preview: Knicks at 76ers, October 5, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Is there really a game already? Oy vey. We are still getting used to how brief the summer break is when the basketball team you cover is actually successful in the postseason.

Indeed, the NBA champion New York Knicks open their preseason schedule tonight. They’ll travel to face a Philadelphia 76ers club that has bolstered its own championship aspirations this summer. What was a solid but flawed Eastern Conference contender now features LeBron James and Jaylen Brown alongside Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and sophomore VJ Edgecombe, assembling one of the most star-studliest lineups in the league.

For the defending champions, this scrimmage will be the first peek at what Mike Brown hopes to tweak for the upcoming season. The second-year coach has already stressed that he intends to ease his core into the exhibition slate. They had a short summer recess, after all. Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, OG () Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns will not shoulder heavy workloads right away, which should open the door for extended looks at the players still fighting for roster security and rotation minutes. Additionally, sophomore Mohamed Diawara will be challenged to prove that he’s ready for a leap after a promising first season and fizzling out in summer league.

We’ll be focused on the center position where the coaching staff is still sorting out depth behind Towns and former Sixer Andre Drummond. Journeymen James Wiseman, Tony Bradley, and Drew Eubanks are all competing in camp for the third-string spot, and Monday’s game affords them a chance to show how they stack up against Embiid and ex-Knick Ariel Hukporti.

As for the health of New York’s starters, Hart continues to play with a damaged digit, and Brunson has reportedly looked sharp in camp after recovering from wrist surgery. Meanwhile, there’s an undercurrent of unresolved contracts, with Towns, Hart, and Miles McBride all eligible for veteran extensions. Because they are in (or effectively in) the final year of their deals—McBride on an expiring contract, Towns with a $61M player option for 2027-28, and Hart with a $22.4M team option for 2027-28—they can negotiate and sign extensions at any point until June 30, 2027. All three have expressed interest in buttoning up their paperwork sooner than that, but this seems like the storyline that will hang over the entire season.

For the Fightin’ Cheesesteaks, our curiosity centers around how coach Nick Nurse will get James, Brown, Embiid, and Maxey to share the ball and defend consistently. We expect their early games to have some of the confusion of an All-Star game, when the alphas try to figure out who will be less-alpha on any given play.

Really, the primary goal of a preseason game is “Don’t break nothin.” You won’t see Captain Brunson take a charge tonight, or Hart do anything that could make his finger fall off. New York swept the Liberty Bells in the second round of the playoffs, as part of a 13-game win streak, and while tonight’s opponent has improved, neither club wants to reveal its tricks in a meaningless contest. They’ll save the good stuff for opening night, when they clash on banner night at Madison Square Garden. Still, it will be fun to see our champs take the floor again. And so soon. Prediction: Knicks by six.

items.title: ‘In one moment I was really believing it’ - disappointed Giulio Ciccone reflects on agonising second place at European Championships
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Giulio Ciccone raced a near-perfect race at the UEC European Road Championships on Sunday, not only being the only rider able to follow Remco Evenepoel’s attacks but also able to capitalise on the fact that his teammate was chasing. He stayed with the Belgian all the way to the finish, setting up a two-up sprint for the title.

Unsure who had won, the pair waited past the finish line until the result was announced. Ciccone bowed his head while Evenepoel, nearby, let out a joyful scream.

He could not hide his disappointment on the podium and while talking to the media afterwards.

“I feel really really disappointed. But first I want to say congrats to Remco, super strong ride,” Ciccone told .

Letting the Belgian squad control the front of the pack, Ciccone waited, and then covered Evenepoel’s first attack on the Možjanca climb with 36 kilometres to go. When the Belgian overcooked a corner and slid out, Ciccone eased off and waited for the peloton.

But he was ready for the next attack, coming only four kilometres later. The pair pulled away from the pack, gaining time, and then Ciccone refused to work when he found out that his teammate was chasing behind with 14 kilometres to go.

“I also was lucky with the situation in the race with [Christian] Scaroni alone behind us. So I also played on the situation to stay on the wheel. I understand that for him was not a nice situation in the front, but this is the race situation.”

Racing a total of five times around the circuit, Ciccone had time to plan his approach the final corner before the finish line.

“I was thinking in my head how to do it, and I was in the last few kilometres. I was just thinking about this corner, and I was thinking to take the first position, but then he understood my plan, and he made the acceleration just before.”

But Evenepoel took a wide line through the final corner, leaving the inside open for Ciccone, who immediately accelerated and briefly opened up a few metres.

“Then my plan was just go full after the corner. In one moment I was really believing it. But then, yeah, this is the race, and it's like this.”

It was the ninth podium finish this year.

“I think it's one of the hardest years of my career. I don't know how many times I've finished second or on the podium. Eight, nine, or I don't know how many times.”

“Today I think was really close, but then another time second. So now for the last two races, I just want to you know, race without pressure and let's see what just to enjoy the bike.”

Ciccone will line up at Il Lombardia, the fifth and final monument of the year next weekend.

items.title: ‘My Shape Is Really Bad’: Tadej Pogačar Sorry/Not Sorry to Miss Euro Champs

items.content: Speculation growing about when and where Pogačar could return to racing in 2027. His team and others comment.

items.title: New WRC champion Evans relieved after “surreal” Sardinia title showdown
‘I know my shape is kind of really bad’- Tadej Pogačar comes to terms with missing European Championships in Slovenia
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
But, of course, Pogačar still returned home to soak up the cheers. Riding in the race director’s car, he waved to fans lining the road on the Možjanca climb and gathered at the finish in Šenčur.

The UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider said he had no regrets about sitting out the race, but admitted he felt differently two weeks earlier, just weeks after crashing out of the Vuelta a España.

“I'm here riding my bike for one week now outside [since the crash], and I know my shape is kind of really bad, and I don't wish to be riding out today,” he told with a chuckle.

“A week or two ago, though, I was really eager to be on the start today.”

But it was a tougher call for his fiancée, Urška Žigart, who refractured her jaw in a crash at Faun Tour Femmes in September. The AG Insurance-Soudal rider was also forced to miss Saturday’s women’s race on home soil.

“Even yesterday, when we were watching a women's race, Urška was like, ‘ah, damn, I should be there’, and she's been feeling super good,” Pogačar said. “When you have good shape. It's tough to look at the race and know that you could be part of it.”

“Luka has been a big part of my career,” said Pogačar who was present at Mezgec biggest win of his career, when he was around 15 years old at the 2014 Giro d’Italia in Trieste.

“Since then, he was kind of my idol and mentor in the national team, and I learned a lot from him. And he had a really amazing career. I think a lot of young kids, young cyclists, should aim more to have a career like him as a lead-out man and a helper and a road captain in the team," he added. "So to be here today with him is really nice and I'm honoured to be sitting next to him.”

Mezgec went out in style, going into the early break and then high-fiving the crowd once he was caught before calling it a day.

items.title: Was it 'unfair' not to penalise stricken F1 cars in Malaysia?
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Fernando Alonso believes it was unfair that the stricken cars were allowed to start Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as "they never stopped a race" for an Aston Martin grinding to a halt this year.

There was chaos at the attempted start of F1's first race in Malaysia in nine years as several cars encountered issues, crawling or coming to a halt, for what's now been diagnosed as a "software bug" with the 2026 power units.

But it did not affect Alonso's Aston Martin Honda. He'd overtaken the ailing Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton and would have taken the restart 11th, on the fringes of the points. 

But with that start abandoned, the order was reset to that of the starting grid for the next (successful) attempt to start the race - a decision Alonso still wasn't pleased with after the race, despite finishing eighth.  

He said: "I think I had 50% DNF this year. They never stopped the race for us." 

Asked by The Race if it was unfair, Alonso said: "100%. I mean, this is motor racing…if it's a safety concern, I get it. If there are five cars in the middle of the road or whatever, we have to stop the race and we need to see what's going on. 

"But I think they were out of the race. They were out, even on the [start/finish pit]wall. They had to push it two metres, the marshals, and retire the car - like we do in 50% of the races. 

"It's the first time I see it, but right now I don't have all the info, so maybe there is a clear explanation and it's OK. I'm not too concerned."

What was going through his mind when he saw other cars stranded?

Alonso said: "The same thing that goes through their mind when they see the Aston Martin stop, I guess. Sad on one side because they have a problem, good because you have one car less in the race."

Alonso was speaking before the FIA publicly explained that there was a software bug. It sent a software update for all teams to download before the actual race start, so it's possible he'll revise his opinion in the days to come now he knows the cause of the problem.

The key difference to Alonso's DNFs - he's retired from 37.5% of grands prix this year - is that they have all been down to Aston Martin Honda's own reliability issues. The software glitch issue that struck the likes of Hamilton was an issue with an FIA-supplied software, outside of the team or drivers' control.

There are specific regulations over starting procedures being suspended, as was the case after the formation lap chaos. 

Article B5.14.1 of the FIA's sporting regulations says: "If at any time after the formation laps behind the safety car have commenced, track conditions are considered unsuitable to start the [session], the message "STARTING PROCEDURE SUSPENDED" will be sent to all competitors.

"Red flags will be shown at all marshal posts and at the control line, and the orange lights on the start gantry will be illuminated. 

"All F1 cars must enter the pitlane behind the safety car. 

"The first F1 car to arrive in the pitlane should proceed directly to the pitlane exit…All the other F1 cars should form up in a line behind the first F1 car in the order they entered the pitlane behind the safety car when the starting procedure was suspended."  

But that order is subject to change by the time the race is properly restarted, which is what allowed Hamilton to reclaim his second place.

There are rules around "Any driver who caused an aborted start and is then subsequently able to start must start from the end of the pitlane", but this didn't apply to Hamilton because the start was aborted for multiple drivers' issues, outside of their or their cars' control. 

So it could have been a different story had Hamilton spun off by himself and caused the suspended start. Instead a common-sense decsion was taken to reset things.

Aston Martin's chief trackside officer Mike Krack called it "a difficult subject" when The Race put Alonso's comments to him.

"I think it was really the only thing the FIA could have done at that point. The race had not started, so this was the formation lap. The race had not started, and they aborted.

"Obviously, we need to review the whole thing. It was a bit chaotic. I think for everyone, nobody really knew what was going on.

"But, at the end of the day, if you zoom out, I think it was the right thing to do." 

Mercedes would have also benefited as Hamilton's demise would have been a place gained for both Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, but deputy team boss Bradley Lord felt the right decision was made. 

"I think it was a slightly unprecedented situation," Lord said. 

"Likewise, formally speaking, the starting procedure hadn't happened, we were in the middle of formation laps before a call had been made, and so it felt like the, in the moment maybe if you felt advantaged or disadvantaged, it felt right or wrong, but overall it was the common sense thing to do.

"If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled-up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and was behind the safety car on a formation lap.

"I think that would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did, and it was pretty exciting when that happened."

items.title: Solberg has no regrets after WRC title near-miss: “It hurts a lot”
Charm City Cross Day 1: Manon Bakker and Tofik Beshir take solo victories in C1 races
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Manon Bakker and Tofik Beshir (CXD Trek Bikes) soloed to win the C1 races of Charm City Cross in Baltimore, Maryland, on day 1 of the third round of the 2026 US Cyclocross Series (USCX). Each rider took their fourth victory in five races in the series on Saturday.

In the women’s race, Bakker leaned into the same strategy that has served her well throughout the series, leading from the first lap. Bakker was coming off her first loss of the season on Day 2 at GO Cross.

“Today, I had a lot better focus and made no mistakes in the race,” Bakker said.

Lauren Zoerner led the front group going up the decisive Mansion Hill and across the long off-camber section on lap one. Going into the downhill, Bakker saw an opportunity to create some space ahead of her USCX rival, Sidney McGill.

From that point on, Bakker was untouchable. Behind her, McGill, Zoerner, Mia Aseltine (Competitive Edge Racing), Nico Knoll (PRO.FWD) and Kaya Musgrave (Competitive Edge Racing) formed the early chase, but the demanding course quickly turned the race into a war of attrition. Just past the halfway point of the six-lap race, McGill and Aseltine had emerged together in the battle for the remaining podium spots.

With two laps to go, McGill gapped Aseltine on the climb and rode on to secure second place, crossing the line 34 seconds behind the winner. Aseltine was third, a further 14 seconds down.

“I overtook Lauren right before the corner, going back down, and I knew that, normally, she couldn't hold my wheel,” Bakker added. “Probably Sydney is the only one who can. So, I wanted to have somebody in between me and Sydney to make it a little bit harder for her.”

The elite men’s race marked a homecoming for 19-year-old Beshir, who first lined up at Charm City six years ago during his inaugural cyclo-cross season. Baltimore is also the hometown of Marc Frazer, who mentored Beshir early in his career as team director at Kelly Benefits Strategies Cycling.

“To win in his hometown—that’s special,” Beshir says. “He’s the one that got me into the sport and it really means a lot to me.”

Struggling to return to form since an injury earlier in the year, Pan-American champion Andrew Strohmeyer (Competitive Edge Racing) put in a massive acceleration from the start, building a gap of 15 seconds to his closest pursuers by the third lap.

Beshir, who had been forced to fight his way through traffic after crashing on a corner earlier in the race, chased solo before finally catching Strohmeyer and settling onto his wheel. But a tiring Strohmeyer soon dropped back to the chase group, where he joined teammates Ryan Drummond and Dylan Zakrajsek, along with Tyler Clark (Caledon Hills Cycling Armada) and Miles Mattern (CXD Trek Bikes). Beshir continued alone with three laps to go.

One lap later, Clark attacked the group and crossed the line 18 seconds behind the winner for second place. The battle for third place heated up the final time up Mansion Hill, where Zakrajsek was able to pull away and hold on for third place.

“I knew Strohmeyer wasn’t going to slow down because he’s legit,” Beshir said. “I knew I needed to pull him back slowly. I didn’t want to burn myself out.”

“I wanted to follow him [Strohmeyer] because he is incredible,” he added. “I know he's not having a great season, but, just following him, you can tell he has a lot of experience and I've always admired him. I was definitely excited to follow his lines and learn new things from him.”

The UCI C2 race on day two at Charm will create some different dynamics, as parts of the course will be reversed and overnight rain could create slick conditions. Series champions will be officially crowned, as Sunday’s race will be the finale of the three-event series.

items.title: Tour de Vendée: Alexis Renard sprints to first professional victory of his career
items.author: Lyne Lamoureux
items.content:
Alexis Renard sprinted to victory in the Tour de Vendée, doubling up on wins this week for Cofidis this weekend after his teammate Jenthe Biermans won Cholet Agglo Tour on Saturday. It was the first professional victory for the 27-year-old Frenchman who typically is a lead-out man for Bryan Coquard.

After the final breakaway was caught inside of seven kilometres to go, teams jostled for position on two laps of the 3km finishing circuit featuring three main corners, and peppered with road furniture in between, with Cofidis making a big push to come together as a team before the final decisive corner.

Xabier Berasategi (Euskatel-Euskadi) took second and Giovanni Lonardi (Polti VisitMalta) was third in Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie.

“I was leading Bryan out again today, but I came past him a bit too quickly in the finale; when I launched, or rather, when I intended to launch him, I saw the 200m sign and thought, ‘Right, this should work’,” Renard said.

“I was strong yesterday, too. I broke my derailleur but managed to get back to the peloton from a long way back. So, we had high ambitions this weekend for the team and Bryan, and that I’m the one who won today is just incredible. It’s my first professional victory, something I’m really going to savour.”

 Renard and his teammate Paul Ourselin has made their way into an early 18-rider breakaway that escaped after some 50 kilometres of racing.

 “Honestly, I thought it [the break] was going to go to the end, but TotalEnergies wasn't rolling so it's a bit disorganised. In the end, we tried to re-mobilise with Jenthe and Bryan to try to lead him out. Finally I managed to get the victory, so it stays in the team and that’s always good.”

Clément Venturini (Unibet Rose Rockets) secured the FDJ United Series title for the second consecutive year, finishing 15th in the 13th and final races of the season. The series was formerly known as the Coupe de France.

Starting in Saint-Jean-d’Hermine, the 198.2km course passed through several villages before reaching a landmark of Vendée cycling: Chantonnay and its famous "Côte du Gîte" climb, which has played a pivotal role in several French National Championships. The peloton then headed west to the seaside resort of Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie, a first-time coastal finish for the Tour de Vendée. The finale was contested over two large 10km laps, followed by three shorter 3km laps.

A number of large groups tried to get away in the early kilometres, but a split in the bunch finally allowed a huge break to form, with 18 riders, including Renard, quickly building a lead of more than a minute, with 50km ridden.

The gap hovered around the one-minute mark for the large group before they were reeled in after spending 87 kilometres off the front. Two riders, Léandre Huck (Van Rysel Roubaix) and Enzo Paleni (Groupama-FDJ United), countered and pulled away only to be reeled in after the first small lap.

The two French WorldTour teams, Decathlon CMA CGM and Groupama-FDJ United, put riders at the front, but it was hard to control the pace in the criterium-style finale.

items.title: 'Finished the season on a high' – Riley Pickrell and Modern Adventure reap the rewards of a season of building the lead out at Le Tour de Langkawi
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It may not have been another stage victory on Sunday's final day of racing at Le Tour de Langkawi for Riley Pickrell (Modern Adventure) but, once again, it wasn't that far off in a tour where the consistency of the Canadian's presence in the top two spots has delivered a clear reminder of just how far the squad has come in the space of 12 months.

Pickrell has undoubtedly been impressive in his turn of speed, though he is far from taking sole credit for the three second places and one win he gathered from the four sprint contests that unfolded at the Malaysian ProTour race this week. And there was also a fifth place when he sprinted from the group after the break had already soaked up the top four spots.

"If I have consistency, it means my teammates are always dropping me off in a good position where I can sprint to a top three," Pickrell told s after the race finale in Putrajaya. "So this week I can really only say thanks to my team because they're the reason why it's so consistent."

That hasn't always been the case, as given Modern Adventure ProTeam is only in its first season it meant that they were starting fresh, and had to find their feet both together as a team and also within the peloton and it's a process that clearly continued through the eight-day tour.

"We didn't have this kind of consistency at the beginning of this year because we had never worked with each other before," explained Pickrell. "We didn't have the processes. We have spent so many hours post-race being pretty critical on where we've made mistakes in these lead outs and how to read the read the race better.

"So now when we're exposed to those situations again and again, we know what the other rider wants out of it and how to adjust accordingly. And that's why the consistency is really coming out. I'm super excited for next year. Most of us here are going into offseason now but we definitely finished the season on a high and I think all the guys are really eager to already get started for next season."

There was more to being satisfied with the outcome than the consistent top placings, there was a first win of the season for Pickrell and sixth for the squad. It also went beyond the improvements within the team lead-out, as this race perhaps felt a little more like a coming of age.

As sports director Alex Howes put it just before the squad pulled off the win on stage 6, "We're figuring stuff out as a team so honestly, we're just happy to be in a position where we get to have this conversation about beating a team like Astana. They're a good team and we have got a lot of respect for them, but I think we can get around them."

Then when they did, XDS Astana clearly didn't consider it a fluke, as they were determined to put the responsibility for the chase of the break on the new squad's shoulders after they had won a stage

"We kind of went into this season kind of being like 'we're just gonna be like the little shit team that nobody respects and it's gonna be really hard to do anything' whereas I really feel like by the end of this season we have a lot of respect," Pickrell said, adding that if the team wasn't respected XDS-Astana would never have tried to hand over the responsibility for chasing down the break to the squad.

"I think that says a lot for what we've accomplished this year and the trajectory we are on is really impressive."

items.title: Remco Evenepoel to skip the European Championships time trial to concentrate on next Sunday's Il Lombardia
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Recently crowned time trial World Champion Remco Evenepoel is to skip the defence of his European title to concentrate on winning Il Lombardia, he revealed on Sunday.

"Wednesday? No, no, I'm going to focus on Lombardia now," he responded when the interviewer said he’d see the Belgian star on Wednesday for the TT.

Evenepoel is without doubt the best time trialist of the current era, not only does he have four rainbow jerseys to his name, but he’s won the European title twice, including last year in France. He’s also a multiple Belgian champion and, of course, the current Olympic champion after taking gold in Paris, just days before doing the same in the road race.

This week’s Slovenian course would certainly have suited the 26-year-old, covering as it does the same 22km lap on which he won Sunday’s road race, but he clearly has other priorities.

Though he has two Monument victories to his name, winning Liège-Bastogne-Liège in both 2022 and 2023, he has never won Il Lombardia, instead finishing the last two editions behind Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), with three other participations dating back to 2020.

However, with Pogačar still recovering from the injuries he sustained in a crash on stage 8 of the Vuelta a España, Evenepoel has the perfect opportunity to add the Italian Classic to his palmarès.

There had been rumours Pogačar was to start the European Championships road race in Slovenia on Sunday, but he was unable to take the start despite it being in his home country. He was, however, at the race to see Evenepoel win, waving to crowds from one of the race direction cars. Evenepoel will certainly be hoping he doesn’t change his mind.

Evenepoel's ride to win the European road race was an excellent one. His Belgian team did much of the riding and covered any threatening move all day long. He then managed to catch Giulio Ciccone after crashing, then did most of the work to take the pair to the line.

Before his appointment in Il Lombardia, Evenepoel has something else on his mind, "I’m gonna celebrate tonight because it's a special one. Like I said, it's now I won all the championships in pro cycling, so I think this one we can celebrate it big time."

items.title: Winners and losers from F1's 2026 Bahrain GP in Malaysia
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
A very strange start was followed by a race full of curveballs in Formula 1's 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix, held in Malaysia.

Here's our pick of the stars and flops.

Winner: Max Verstappen & Red Bull (1st)

A first pole and win of the season for Red Bull, its engine division and the absolute star of today's show, Max Verstappen.

He was almighty at every turn today. He completed a lovely, intricate move at Turns 1-3 around the outside of Kimi Antonelli early on, was absolutely rapid as the track dried, and - after a briefly alarming moment when he stopped late on and lost the lead before the Mercedes followed suit a lap later - held off Antonelli for the win.

While you wouldn't expect to see Isack Hadjar on par with Verstappen, the gap between the two Red Bulls today shows the level at which Verstappen is operating in these scenarios. The car helped, but the driver made the ultimate difference.

And a word for Red Bull Powertrains. Both Audi and Honda (for Aston Martin) have had engine struggles this year. RBPT has produced what is F1's best internal combustion engine at its very first attempt, so that's a big positive for future years as it improves its battery and deployment abilities.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (5th)

The obvious loss for Hadjar here is being mugged by both Ferraris on the four-lap shootout after the safety car at the end.

However, look earlier and the problems were already there. He was jumped by Liam Lawson at the start, and after he got that place back he rarely matched team-mate Verstappen's pace. He was as much as three seconds per lap slower at times even when he had a certain amount of clean air.

We're not expecting Verstappen-level performances from Hadjar less than two years into his F1 career, but he looked like he was driving a different brand of car today.

Remember two safety cars reset the field. He was almost 10 seconds behind Verstappen at the lap nine safety car, and 28s behind before the one on lap 42.

Loser: George Russell (classified 20th)

Such a deeply nasty ending to what was already a disappointing-but-manageable weekend.

Even before the 'grand finale' of losing third in the final laps due to a power unit issue, George Russell had suffered a couple of ignominies at Sepang - one was the qualifying defeat to Mercedes team-mate Antonelli (who was limited to one Q3 run), the other was being reeled in and overtaken by Antonelli with what looked like unbefitting ease.

If anything, the late-race issue can almost soothes a little what had come before - because there's nothing you can do. Just wasn't his weekend. Just isn't his year.

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (3rd)

Merely changing Lewis Hamilton's tyres to inters at the start may have made him a victory contender, but watching the laptimes during the race I don't think Hamilton had an answer for Verstappen or Antonelli, especially with Hamilton's ill-chosen stint on the poorer mediums, so really I believe this was the best result possible even if Hamilton reckons second was doable.

I think it would be fair to criticise another Ferrari mismanagement of a race though, because the inters were the right choice. It was only a Hamilton masterclass and a bit of luck elsewhere away from barely breaching the points.

Hamilton carved through from 16th to fifth in the second stint after a great call to stay out on his original softs and not switch to new ones under the first safety car.

Then he reduced an 11 second gap to Hadjar down to 3.5s before stopping, struggled on the mediums then nailed a pass on the faster Red Bull shortly after the final safety car when back on his favoured softs. Unbelievable performance.

Team-mate Charles Leclerc had to overcome an extra stop, for the inters early on, but when things were level he took much longer to fight through the pack than Hamilton did. He was about 15s behind before the final safety car, but getting to fourth was still a very nice recovery. One you might celebrate if Hamilton hadn't done what he did.

Loser: Williams (17th & DNF)

In a race where it ran sixth and seventh early on with the correct choice of inters at the start, everything pretty much fell apart for Williams under the first safety car caused by Valtteri Bottas's spin on lap nine.

In the double-stack pitstop which followed for Williams, Alex Albon was the second car and had to wait for his stop, costing him three positions.

Carlos Sainz, in the leading car, was tagged by Gabriel Bortoleto on the restart. A hilarious radio sequence followed where Bortoleto said Sainz left him no room and Sainz said he left all the room in the world. The 10-second penalty for Bortoleto showed the stewards' opinion on it.

That left Sainz struggling to recover from the back, and Albon was well out of reach of the points in 19th when his gearbox later broke.

Winner: Fernando Alonso (8th)

It felt like there was never any doubt, once the restart order had taken shape during the final safety car, that Fernando Alonso would score 'something' for Aston Martin. 

He is still the go-to man on the grid when it comes to a situation like that - and the only question was whether he would be able to fend off the McLaren of Lando Norris, which, of course, he was.

It's a big result for Aston Martin (not just because Alonso was over a minute off five laps in due to the starting tyre call), and a big example of the value its star driver brings when you need to simply keep the programme afloat.

Clearly, the AMR26 has improved - but things would sure have looked a lot bleaker in the results table without Alonso's endless opportunism.

Loser: Alpine (13th and 16th) 

No intra-team collision this time for Alpine but a “very painful” couple of wrong tyre calls across both cars, which left Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly well outside the top 10. 

Gasly explained: “We thought the track could dry a lot quicker. The team was willing to take the gamble, I supported it because, to me, it sort of made sense, and our worst-case scenario was still a lot better than, unfortunately, what the reality was. 

“When we went out there, we're losing a huge amount of laptime, and then it's a choice of coming back on your decision or trying to stay out there and make it work. But we tried that and unfortunately it cost us a lot of laptime. 

“Then after the virtual safety car, we had the safety car, and everything went the other way; nothing really came our way. We never could capitalise on anything, and it was just very painful.” 

Painful because Racing Bulls scooped seven points and extended its advantage over Alpine in their battle for fifth in the championship to 22 points.

Winner: Racing Bulls (7th and 10th)

OK, so things didn’t end as well as they started for Racing Bulls, considering Liam Lawson was duelling with Verstappen for the final place on the podium on the opening lap, but Lawson still walked away with the top midfield honours. 

That’s despite some frightful formation laps where Lawson didn’t have team radio.

“I knew I had no radio before I even pulled away for the formation lap, so I was very stressed because there's a lot of procedures, especially in this year's car, that you have to do, and I literally was like, no idea what's going on, no idea what mode I was meant to be in,” Lawson explained.

“I had to look at my pit board on the way by to read a certain switch change I had to do, and then it brought the radio back. So, yeah, very stressful. 

“That was probably the most alone I've ever felt, and obviously very confusing when all the cars were slowing down, but again, I couldn't talk to the team. I didn't know if I was allowed to overtake or what. Just a lot of confusion.”

Lawson bounced back from that strongly to drive to seventh place with strong pace that made him regret not defending against Oscar Piastri’s McLaren harder. 

Team-mate Arvid Lindblad picked up the final point late on by passing Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi.

Loser: Audi (11th and 18th) 

The upgraded Audi performed much better at Sepang than it did in Baku, with Bortoleto making it into Q3, but that progress didn’t translate into any points.

Bortoleto misjudged how wet Turn 2 was and went steaming into Sainz’s Williams, picking up damage on his car as well as a 10-second time penalty that ruined any chance of points.

Audi made the wrong call fitting Hulkenberg with slicks at the start, something he admitted was “too ambitious”, but that was quickly rectified with a move back to the intermediates.

It then got the timing right to go back to slicks, but the safety car coming out right after that nullified its advantage from doing so.

“I was eating my steering wheel at that,” was how Hulkenberg described his feelings. “That sucked because I was feeling brave and like a hero in that moment.

“I think we could have undercut a few people, but unfortunately, the safety car had other plans.”

Hulkenberg ultimately ended up finishing 11th - the ninth time an Audi has finished there this season.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (2nd)

A couple of high-profile errors at Turn 15 made Verstappen's job easier today, but Antonelli's Mercedes wasn't as fast as the Red Bull and the outcome was successfully being best of the rest and extending his points lead.

That's up to 84 now, and while the race was a bit scruffy, it didn't affect the outcome. Team-mate Russell's retirement only adds to the impending feeling that Antonelli is within reach of a first title.

Even if Russell hadn't retired, Antonelli had caught and passed Russell to show he was the quicker and better driver on the day, and even if Russell hadn't retired, it wouldn't change the expectation of where the title's going, he still would have extended his lead.

Loser: Esteban Ocon (15th)

Esteban Ocon has been in strong form lately and he made the most of starting on the correct intermediate tyre for the start to jump well into the top 10 from 17th - all after he'd pulled over to the side on the original formation lap which could have ruined his race.

He made quick work of the two Williams as well, overtaking them on merit in the early running to go as high as sixth in a "mega" stint.

But that was as good as it got as the track dried and the relative pace of the Haas showed. Spirited battles, but faster cars came through and he returned back down to 15th and behind his Haas team-mate Ollie Bearman again.

Loser: McLaren (6th and 9th) 

Like Ferrari, McLaren got the tyre call wrong at the start of the race, though it at least partly rectified that on Piastri’s side by bringing him into the pits at the end of formation laps to ditch the slick tyres.

But unlike Ferrari, the McLarens didn’t have the raw pace to make the progress it would have liked, looking fourth best and vulnerable to the midfield.

Norris was caught out by the cars ahead of him braking behind Russell’s stricken Mercedes under safety car, but it looked like an avoidable error. 

It was an error that ensured he finished behind Lawson’s Racing Bulls and even Alonso’s Aston Martin Honda. 

And the meagre points tally of 10 means Red Bull is now just 18 points adrift of it in the constructors’ championship, and Verstappen now ties Norris in the drivers' points.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I think he has endless upside’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Paying homage to my biggest brain fart…

Would you believe the Knicks play basketball tomorrow!?

Here’s the latest from around Tarrytown and those places.

On Mohamed Diawara’s increased comfort and development entering Year 2:

“Last year, you could see he was a little jittery when he was out there, because he didn’t quite know what to do, and he knew when he did it, he just had to go hard. So a lot of times, he would just play at one speed. There’s a comfort level now, so his cadence is better, especially offensively. His ability to communicate on the floor is at a little bit of a higher level, because he has a better feel not just offensively, but defensively — not just what he should do, but what he should be telling his teammates to do, especially if he’s on the backside or bottom side of the defense, because he sees everything in front of him. He’s one of those players that needs to take a step forward.”

On his plans for the preseason opener:

“(Starters will play,) but not much. We’ll try to ease them in. The last game is always a dress rehearsal, but we’ll try to build them up leading to that game.”

On accepting preseason mistakes and emphasizing next-play speed:

“Any time you have new guys, because we have new guys on this team that we’re trying to mix in with guys that have been here, you’re gonna make some mistakes. I’m 100 percent OK with that. Once somebody makes a mistake, I’m looking for how quickly do they try to make up for the same mistake? I’m huge on the next-play speed.

“So there’s gonna be a a lot of mistakes, but are guys gonna drop their head a little or hesitate? It happened anyway. Move on, try to correct it. and then address it during the day also.”

On what he’ll prioritize seeing in preseason:

“Overall effort, the little things like boxing out every single time, competing, offensively, to offensive rebound, and then sprinting corner-to-corner in transition.”

On ending practices with a must-make free throw:

“It puts pressure on guys, you know, and then everybody’s standing there watching. So if you miss it, everybody’s got to run. I got it from Pop. It also, at the end of the day, brings the group together.”

On Tony Bradley making the final free throw on Saturday:

“You see everybody came and gave him love. So you feel good when you do it.”

On being followed home by a family of Knicks fans after the championship:

“I stopped at the red light. The first vehicle was kind of honking at me and I could see the kids waving out. So I go through and they turn into a driveway three or four houses past the red light and the father and kids jump out of the car and start waving and they had their Knicks gear on and I gave them a wave.

“But I had my helmet and my sunglasses, so I didn’t think anybody noticed me. So I ride home and I’ve got my country music blasting, and I pull into my driveway in my garage, and the next thing you know, that car was pulling into my driveway. They followed me home.

“I don’t know how they got back in their car that quickly and followed me home. But they followed me home. And the guy owns a company and he had some food products, so he brings out a box of cereal and all that. And he’s got his three kids and they just start telling me what the championship meant . . .

“This is like August, two months after the championship, but you could still feel that passion. So was it scary? Yes. It was scary. Any time you get followed home, it is very, very scary, but just to see the joy and excitement, especially on kids’ faces.

“The dad was more excited than the kids, by the way, but to see that, you realize this is not just a championship. This is special.”

On falling out of the Knicks’ rotation during his rookie season:

“Honestly, It didn’t really need explanation. I think I was a rookie. That was my first year. So you just got to be ready, whatever the team wants you to do. We have a great team with big players, so if I was in the rotation and I’m not in the rotation anymore, I think it’s just part of the game for the whole team. I wasn’t really thinking about that, I was just ready to take any opportunity. I wasn’t thinking about not playing and stuff.”

On better understanding how to prepare his body for the NBA:

“Now that I know a little bit more the physicality that I need in the league, how I need to prepare my body. … I think now that I have a year in the league, it’s a little bit easier to see how I can prepare for the new season.”

On the Knicks’ championship parade and his offseason:

“I always knew Knicks fans were another kind of fans…I was prepared for it to be a big thing. But I was surprised, it was great to see.

“Best summer of my life… went back to Paris, it was nice. Everybody was happy about it.”

On Mohamed Diawara’s potential:

“I think he has endless upside. He’s very talented, can do a lot: shoot, defend, pass. He can do everything; a really versatile player. I’m excited to see him grow. I think he’s going to keep getting better and better, so I’m really excited for him.”

On receiving the key to his hometown of Jefferson City:

“Yeah, they just told me they were going to do it. I grew up in Jeff City, went to high school out there, have lifelong friends, and I just — I grew up there.

“So Jeff City, Missouri is special to me. So it’s an honor.”

On believing more recognition will come after the Knicks’ championship run:

“Throughout the season, that’s where more recognition will come. This next season, I think I put it on display every night, the versatility, being able to guard anyone and affect the game offensively and defensively. I’m a two-way player, that’s what I take pride in, helping the team win games. I think I’ve always done it.

“Maybe there’s more of an eye on it right now because we just won the championship. That’s what I pride myself in.”

On Mike Brown’s coaching chops:

“He deserves all the praise… he’s always been a great coach. When you win, you get more recognition. Everything is coming together for him.”

On his work with Pacome Dadiet and Mo:

“I encourage them when they’re doing well… be there for them any way I can.”

“It was fun, we were there for Jalen. Was really cool that he got to host it. We were there for the intro. It was cool to see him do that, some funny skits. It was a good time.”

On not falling for his flowers:

“I really do appreciate it and I respect the hell out of them. It’s honestly really cool and it’s a sign of respect. To hear that from those guys, I really do appreciate it.

“It’s just like a lot of things. When you hear praise, when you hear negativity, it has to go through one ear and out the other. You got to continue to be the best version of yourself or people are going to pass you. I really do appreciate it. It shows where I’ve grown, but still got a lot of work to do.”

Saturday Posted & Toasted Notes: Wise men, French presidents, BrickBron James
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Last weekend without basketball, fellas, so here’s a quick summary of a bunch of stuff that popped up recently around the NBA before we get down to (yeah, I know, , but still…) business.

  • James Wiseman has emerged as the early favorite for the Knicks’ 14th and likely final standard roster spot, according to the New York Post’s Stefan Bondy. Nothing new considering we’ve been talking about New York prioritizing a third center for months on end. In Bondy’s eyes, Tony Bradley and Drew Eubanks are Wiseman’s primary competition up front, while Bruce Brown and Ochai Agbaji are also fighting for the last spot in the Knicks’ roster.
  • Mike Brown, however, isn’t ready to declare Wiseman—or anybody else—the winner of that roster battle.

“I’m just going to let it unfold. I got no expectations. I’m not trying to forecast anything. I’m just taking this literally one practice at a time, one game at a time. And at the end of the day, when it comes time for us to figure out who’s going to be on the final roster, we’ll do it.”

  • The Athletic’s James L. Edwards III identified whether the Knicks can maintain their edge after winning the championship as New York’s biggest question entering the new season.
  • In another piece published over The Athletic, multiple reporters assembled three perspectives on the Knicks’ chances of repeating, and none were especially bullish.
  • Anne Hathaway would sacrifice another Oscar for another Knicks championship.
  • The Pistons and Jalen Duren finally found common ground, with the big boy and postseason no-shower inking a five-year, $200 million deal… without a weight clause on it.
  • Victor Wembanyama hasn’t even won an NBA title, but he’s already thinking about running for President of France.
  • It looks like the Las Vegas Whatevers are a very real thing and will get a franchise approved before Seattle does, but that could come with the con of having to wait an extra year to enter NBA play, contrary to the SuperSonics 2.0 making their comeback in time for the 2028-29 campaign.
  • JaVale McGee has joined the Shanghai Sharks, teaming up with D’Angelo Russell in China. Yes, that’s a real headline.
  • LeBron stans are already aboard the #lbjmvp train. Meanwhile…

items.title: Thrown in with Giggs and Beckham: how Manchester United tried to get Billy Kenny
items.author: Billy Kenny
items.content:
Former Everton midfielder, known as the ‘Goodison Gazza’, recalls being made to feel special by Alex Ferguson in this autobiography extract

“So this is the scouser ya been goin’ on aboot then …” My face turned Manchester United red. Scanning the room full of smiles and staring eyes, I identified the mystery Scottish voice as the man who’d just become the first player to score more than 20 league goals for the club since George Best in the 1960s. “Good answer,” replied Brian McClair after following up on my smile and nod by asking whether I supported Everton or Liverpool. “Ye’ll dee well ’ere laddie.”

Brian Kidd had just introduced me to the Man United first team by silencing the room to draw attention to my presence. “Lads, this is Billy from up the road,” he said. I was still starstruck from seeing all these famous faces as my chauffeur for the day, Eric Harrison, pulled up in the car park at The Cliff a few minutes earlier. Paul McGrath. Mark Hughes. Bryan Robson. Kevin Moran. Norman Whiteside. I ticked them all off in my head. Thank fuck I was developing an ear for everyday Glaswegian because after a bit of piss-taking from the first-teamers about being a scouser, I found myself standing in an office at the end of a short and narrow corridor, shaking hands with another one.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
My brain melted yesterday, thought it was Sunday, not Thursday.

Anyway, today’s Friday. I guess.

Here’s the latest from Tarrytown as we keep hearing from different Knicks.

On Josh Hart’s injured finger and the toughness it reflects:

“Josh, he’s a handsome young man. But that finger is ugly. So, I don’t look at it. But it adds to his toughness. Josh is a tough son of a gun, man. I can’t even watch when he [shakes his hand], because I’m just like, oh, my gosh I can’t imagine having a finger like that.

“But it just shows who he is. He’s tough but, more importantly, there’s dedication there to wanting to be a great shooter, and you’ve got to put it into work. And he puts in the work, even though his finger’s bothering him. And even though it’s a little crooked, he’s putting in the work to get it right. [Shooting coach] Pete [Patton] and the rest of the coaches are helping him out, and it shows that he can shoot at a high level with the dedication he has in the first place.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff performance boosting his All-Star case:

“It should help him a ton because guys that are quiet naturally, they have a hard time getting the necessary publicity and promotion toward being an All-Star, unless you’re doing something extraordinary and people start talking about it — like OG in the playoffs. So doing it in the playoffs and having people talk about it should have carryover, in my opinion, since he helped us win the championship.

“And he was in the conversation for [NBA] Finals MVP. That should definitely help create calls for him to have a case to be an All-Star this year. He’s still got to go earn it, but he should be in everybody’s conversation from the beginning.”

On Anunoby’s shooting ability:

“He’s not [at Stephen Curry] or [Klay Thompson’s] level but the next tier. He’s way better than I thought.”

On Anunoby’s confidence, shooting and the Knicks’ spacing:

“His confidence is really high. And I thought during the playoffs we did a really good job of touching the paint and taking the right 3s. With OG being 6-foot-7 with long arms, if you’re closing to him with a smaller guy or a guard, it’s going to be good for us because they try to put their best player on Jalen, and sometimes, their best player is a bigger perimeter defender.

“So that means OG may have a smaller guy [defending him]. That’s not impacting him when he shoots the basketball.

“So I think first starts off with him, yes; he’s way better than what I thought. I would categorize him as a great shooter. But more importantly, I thought our spacing and our ability to touch the paint and spray it helped out a lot.”

On his plans for the preseason games:

“We’ll try to ease them in. The last game is always a dress rehearsal, but we’ll try to build them up leading to that game.”

On the Knicks’ conditioning entering camp after a short summer:

“All the guys look like they’re in pretty good shape, especially for a short summer. We have a conditioning test that we did last year and this year that the guys have to pass to get into camp and they all passed it.”

On James Wiseman’s presence at training camp:

“Fantastic human being, fantastic young man…. Good to see him in the gym. When you’re that long and that athletic, with skill – he has skill – there’s a place for you in this league. Sometimes it takes the right moment, the right team, the right situation, all that stuff, to be able to fit someplace and grow. We have a lot of great guys in camp that have potential of impacting us in a lot of different ways throughout the course of the year. He’s definitely one of the many guys that we have that we’re excited about.”

On Tony Bradley after his training camp signing:

“We’re looking for bigs. Tony’s a veteran guy that’s still in his prime and has a good feel for the game, knows how to play the game the right way and he’s hurt us in the past. To be honest, when a guy hurts you in the past, you tend to remember him more than others. So to be able to add him to camp was a positive for us because again, I said this last year, (Karl-Anthony Towns) has one of the most (challenging positions) out of everybody because I want to move him around when I play him at center. I want to play him at power forward; (when he’s at) power forward 1-4 is interchangeable. Same with OG (Anunoby). OG we put him at the 5 last year. We probably will do it a little bit more this year as well.

“But to be able to do that, you’ve gotta have enough centers around on the team, so having Tony here with his skill set and feel is definitely a blessing because we’re looking at that position heavily.”

On the options to fix his finger:

“The only option for my finger at this point, because of how damaged it is, is a full joint replacement. With a joint replacement, you can’t have the banging, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that. You can’t do that. So if I did a joint replacement, then I wouldn’t be able to play. So I guess it’s either wrap it until I retire or cut it off. I guess that’s the other option. That’s really the only alternative: either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation.

“I mean, there was a lot of stuff that I had to get checked, and that was one of them. It was just with how it deteriorated, the joint and the bone and everything, that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully, they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if y’all didn’t realize. So I’m hoping after that joint replacement it can kind of get a little straighter.”

On how the pain in his finger varies from day to day:

“Some days, it’ll be good. Some days it’ll hurt to catch the ball. It varies. I wish I could tell you when I wake up what’s gonna be good, what’s gonna be bad. Somedays it’s good, like a regular functioning finger. And other days it hurts to just close my hand, to make a fist.”

On why a joint replacement would prevent him from playing basketball:

“You can’t have the banging, you know, repetitive, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that; you can’t do that. It was just with how it deteriorated — the joint and the bone and everything — that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if you know y’all didn’t realize.”

On the appearance and functionality of his injured finger:

“I mean, it’s it’s not the prettiest to look at. I would love to have a straight finger, but you know, it works.”

On the physical toll of an NBA career and what fans don’t get:

“I think people think money is everything, and for me, obviously, you want to be compensated fairly for your performance and all that. But at the end of the day, just because you get paid, be blessed in a position to get paid well and take care of our families, [it’s not like] we’re not humans at the same time. I’m sitting here thinking, my knees are aching a little bit, but I want to leave the game and be able to run around and play with my kids when they’re you know 10, 11,12-plus. So that wear and tear, it’s significant to a certain point. If you’re in this league for 14, 15, 16 years, and you see some of these guys that are older, they they got limps, knees are barking, those kind of things. So I think that definitely gets overlooked. But that’s also why I don’t think I’ll play till I’m 40.”

On OG Anunoby’s increased recognition helping his All-Star chances:

“It’s extremely impactful. Obviously, you have to be a gifted and good player to make an All-Star team, but also you have to have the press and all that kind of behind you, bolstering it. So it’s good for people to see how talented he is, how impactful he is on both sides of the ball in the game. So hopefully that recognition will continue throughout this year, and hopefully we’ll be able to get him in.”

On Jalen Brunson’s increased fame following the Knicks title:

“He’s not LeBron, let’s relax.”

On planning to attend Yankees Game 3:

“I think I’m going to be able to get to Game 3. We have a preseason game the next day. So I’m excited, man. I’m excited for New York. Excited for that team.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff success boosting his confidence:

“That’s definitely a boost of confidence going into this year. OG knows how good he is, and we know how good he is. So he’s gonna continue doing what he does.”

On learning the backcourt rule during his late Game 4 possession:

“I learned on the fly. When I watched the video after, they said you can leave the ball in the backcourt but your body can be in the frontcourt – I didn’t know it was a thing until then. I’m glad it worked out.”

On what has allowed the Knicks to embrace their roles:

“We care for each other, we compete, we want to get each other better”

On whether he always planned to return to the Knicks before signing his extension:

“In my mind, yeah. ‘I want to stay here, I want to stay home.’ We had a chance to do that, and we did it.”

On his championship summer:

“My favorite summer of all time”

On This Date in Knicks History: October 2
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Two noteworthy Knicks birthdays today!

Dr. Dick Barnett was born October 2, 1936, in Gary, Indiana. Barnett spent eight seasons with New York, became an All-Star in 1968, and played for both the 1970 and 1973 championship teams. His number 12 hangs in the Garden rafters. He died last year at 88.

Barnett had one of the most unforgettable shots in basketball history. Starting in college (when nicknamed “Dick the Skull”), he became known for contorting his body into a question mark while shooting his jumper, kicking his legs back and telling defenders, “Too late–fall back, baby!” Barnett went on to turn his eccentric shot into more than 15,000 NBA points.

A beloved teammate of Walt Frazier, Barnett was featured in the documentary film, , about his time playing at Tennessee State University for the Tigers. During segregation, the all-Black Tigers won three straight national championships. Captain Barnett tirelessly fought for their recognition, which culminated in their 2019 induction into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame. Watch the doc here, you’ll dig it.

After hanging up his sneakers, Barnett earned an MBA from New York University and then a PhD in education from Fordham University. He taught Sports Management at St. John’s University for four years.

  • 2× NBA champion (1970, 1973)
  • All-ABL First Team (1962)
  • No. 12 retired by New York Knicks
  • 3× NAIA champion (1957–1959)
  • 3× AP Little College All-American (1957–1959)
  • 2× UPI Little College All-American (1958, 1959)
  • 2× NAIA tournament MVP (1958, 1959)

And (feeling like Garrison Keillor here) Tyson Chandler was born today in 1982, in Hanford, California. Chandler came to New York immediately after anchoring Dallas’ 2011 championship defense and became the 2011-12 NBA Defensive Player of the Year, the only Knick ever to take the honor.

Drafted second in 2001, the seven-foot Chandler played for five seasons in Chicago before bouncing from NOLA to Charlotte to Dallas and then the Knicks. After three seasons at MSG, he was sent back to Dallas, then Phoenix, and finished out his 19-year career with the Lakers and Rockets.

Chandler joined the Knicks in December 2011 via a sign-and-trade between multiple teams, which also sent traded Ronny Turiaf, cash, and a 2013 2nd-round draft pick to the Wizards. While there was no denying his talent, Chandler appeared on the injured list often during his tenure here, with a hamstring strain, playoff flu and an upper respiratory infection, a bulging cervical disc (plus related neck spasms and weight loss from illness), and a fractured right fibula.

In June 2014, he and Raymond Felton were traded to the Mavs for José Calderón, Samuel Dalembert, Wayne Ellington, Shane Larkin, a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Thanasis Antetokounmpo was later selected), and a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Cleanthony Early was later selected). (h/t basketball-reference.com)

Chandler concluded his time in New York with averages of 10.2 points, 10.1 rebounds, and 1.2 blocks across 183 games. His career highlights, also from Wikipedia:

  • All-NBA Third Team (2012)
  • NBA Defensive Player of the Year (2012)
  • NBA All-Defensive First Team (2013)
  • 2× NBA All-Defensive Second Team (2011, 2012)
  • First-team Parade All-American (2001)
  • Second-team Parade All-American (2000)
  • McDonald’s All-American (2001)
  • 2× California Mr. Basketball (2000, 2001)

Quite a nice pairing: two Knicks born 46 years apart, one remembered for his offense, the other for defense. Closing my Writer’s Almanac loop, your poem for the day is a personal favorite, “The Bear,” by Galway Kinnell.

Knicks in five. And keep in touch.

items.author: Paul MacInnes
items.content:
It is a symbol of the connection between the fanbase and club, but there is a growing fear executives would prefer stadiums full of one-off tourists

The document known as “the oldest football season ticket in the world” promises its bearer access to every Burnley home game of the 1884-85 season. It is a ticket that predates the Football League by four years, with all the fixtures played against east Lancashire neighbours. All the same, the legend on the ticket carries a stern warning: “This card is not transferable. Any member violating this rule will be at once expelled from the club.”

For Burnley 1884 read Manchester United 2026. While the oldest remaining season ticket is preserved safely at Turf Moor, at Old Trafford 685 season tickets were voided this summer after a club investigation found evidence of their having been resold on the secondary market. United said such practices “undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United”. United fan groups again protested against the actions of the club’s ownership, claiming: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

In the week that 16-year-old Max Dowman has been thrust into the spotlight, it was another teenager who gave us a glimpse of the future in Brighton’s impressive win over Arsenal. Charalampos Kostoulas – nicknamed ‘Babis’ in his homeland, in homage to former Argentina striker Gabriel Batistuta – has already started twice as many Premier League games as he did in his first season in English football, when he was a backup for Danny Welbeck. The 19-year-old repaid Fabian Hürzeler’s faith in him against the reigning champions. Despite his tender years, Kostoulas already possesses the physical attributes to mix it with the best. He caused Gabriel Magalhães and company problems all afternoon, capping it off with a brilliant goal from 25 yards, his third in eight days. “We always knew that he’s capable of scoring goals out of nowhere,” said Hürzeler. “He just has this intrinsic motivation of really improving every day. Carrick’s side were short on inspiration, despite the summer spend in midfield, and the lack of quality in the final third was stark

One of the more damning aspects of Manchester United’s tortured rebuild is their inability to multitask. So much money has been frittered away, pushing United into the ridiculous position of going one position at a time each summer. Last year was all about the attack and the recent window was about central midfield, even though the options at full-back do not look strong enough to cope with a season back in the Champions League.

United remain a listless, drifting operation. The ownership is reviled and the fanbase is becoming increasingly mutinous. It was not just Gary Neville seeing red as he commentated on United’s dismal efforts away to winless Fulham. There was an ominous shift in the mood in the away end at Craven Cottage, summed up by the boos that greeted Michael Carrick substituting Kobbie Mainoo with 10 minutes to go.

items.title: Manchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quit
items.author: Yassin El-Moudden and Daniel Lavelle
items.content:
Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire

Manchester United’s Muslim supporters’ Club (MUMSC) has called for the Premier League side’s co-owner to step down after he made “completely unacceptable” comments during a BBC interview.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe described the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world”.

items.title: Heat is on Carrick but Wilcox must share blame for Manchester United’s woes
items.author: Will Unwin
items.content:
Recruitment is under scrutiny after £155m was spent on three midfielders while other positions were neglected

There was a mix of boos and apathy as Manchester United slumped out of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday in their latest depressing act in domestic cup competitions. A solemn Michael Carrick and his players were the target for the jeers. The director of football, Jason Wilcox, looked unamused on his way out of the directors’ box but he and the hierarchy need to accept responsibility for their actions.

This is the natural course of football, where supporters know what is good or bad and give a rapid opinion to those whose wages they deem they pay. Carrick and his charges are the face of the club, the ones put up to speak with journalists and sent to promote the wares of sponsors.

items.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Spurs and Villa meet in desperation derby and Andoni Iraola faces test on south-coast return

Chelsea have not won this west London derby since Brentford’s first Premier League season. Each visit since October 2021’s 1-0 win, Ben Chilwell the scorer, has been a draw. This season has continued the divergence between the clubs’ respective approaches, Brentford’s solidity and continuity contrasting with Chelsea attempting their latest reboot. Kevin Schade, after two well-taken goals at Bournemouth, will fancy facing a defence not yet attuned to Xabi Alonso’s configurations. Only one team has won a Premier League title with a defensive trio: Chelsea’s last title team, in 2016-17 under Antonio Conte. Alonso’s attack has been rather more successful, presenting another challenge for Jannik Schuster. Replacing Nathan Collins, the 20-year-old central defender had a tough examination from Bournemouth’s Evanilson on his first Premier League start, emerging with credit. For Chelsea, João Pedro has three goals and three assists, but doubts surrounding his fitness could lead to Danny Welbeck’s first league start.

Brentford v Chelsea, Friday 8pm (all times BST)

Tottenham v Aston Villa, Saturday 12.30pm

items.title: De Cuyper and Brighton pile on pain for Manchester United with comeback
items.author: Jamie Jackson at Old Trafford
items.content:
Across four days Manchester United have lost the 199th derby against Manchester City, were told by JJ Gabriel that he wants to leave, and now they have been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton.

Capitulating after being 2-0 up may be the pick of these dizzying blows, as the prolonged boos at the final whistle suggested, and doing so ends a proud 50-year record: the last time the same lead at Old Trafford ended in defeat was Tottenham’s 3-2 win in September 1976.

items.title: Manchester United shocked as talented youngster JJ Gabriel asks to leave
items.author: Dominic Booth
items.content:
• 15-year-old wants his registration to be cancelled

  • He was to be in squad to face Brighton on Wednesday

Manchester United have been left confused and shocked by the news that the talented 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave the club, a day before he was to be included in the first-team squad to face Brighton.

Gabriel could have become United’s youngest player in the Carabao Cup third-round tie at Old Trafford on Wednesday. But the Guardian understands he has asked for his registration to be cancelled.
